papers.title: Scenario-Based Risk Certificates for Multi-Property Vulnerability Discovery in Parametric MDPs
papers.summary: Safety-critical systems such as network protocols and distributed algorithms depend on environmental parameters whose exact values are uncertain. Parametric Markov decision processes (pMDPs) model such systems by making transition probabilities symbolic functions of the parameters. For a single quantitative requirement, parametric verification asks which parameter valuations satisfy the requirement. In practice, however, engineers often monitor several safety and performance requirements at once, and one valuation may make several requirements vulnerable simultaneously. In this paper we study multi-property vulnerability discovery under requirement-wise semantics: given a pMDP and M quantitative requirements, we construct candidate regions of the parameter space that may contain violations, and study budgets for random testing under a specified parameter distribution. To solve this, we adopt a two-layered approach in which the scenario-approximation layer provides PAC guarantees on identifying conservative vulnerability regions for each requirement while the testing layer treats random parameter exploration as coverage of overlapping regions and yields a stopping certificate computed from the marginal region masses alone; a composition theorem then bounds the expected non-discovery score by the scenario approximation error plus the testing risk from the two layers. For confirmed discoveries, candidate hits are checked by model checking and budgets use independently certified discovery probabilities. Experiment evaluate these certificates using empirical surrogates and independent confidence bounds.

papers.title: VAMR: Multi-Question Agentic Reasoning for Efficient Long-Form Video Understanding
papers.summary: Long-form video understanding often involves multiple questions about different aspects of the same recording. papers.title: Conversing with a Conversational Agent: A Real Conversation, Not a Simulated One
papers.summary: The claim that interactions with artificial conversational agents merely simulate human conversation rests on a philosophical distinction between reproducing the observable features of an activity and actually performing it. Although this distinction is appropriate for certain physical phenomena, its application to linguistic and symbolic activities is far less straightforward. This article argues that conversations with large language model (LLM)-based agents are genuine conversational activities rather than mere simulations, without thereby attributing consciousness, subjective understanding, or human intentionality to artificial systems. Drawing on the distinction between subjective and objective simulation, the article first examines the limitations of defining conversation exclusively through the intrinsic properties of its participants. It then develops a relational and semiotic account of conversational activity, informed by linguistic pragmatics, Lacan's Conversing with a Conversational Agent theory of the mirror, Baudrillard's concept of the simulacrum, Simondon's philosophy of individuation, and Peirce's semiotics. These perspectives make it possible to distinguish the reality of conversational interaction from the appearance of artificial subjectivity and from the epistemic validity of the meanings produced. The argument culminates in the concept of Hybrid Semiotic Fabrication, which characterizes meaning-making as a distributed process involving human participants, artificial intelligence, corpora, and technical arrangements. Recognizing the reality of human-AI conversation therefore entails neither anthropomorphizing artificial agents nor granting their outputs epistemic authority. Rather, it requires a more precise account of the relational, semiotic, and normative conditions under which conversational meaning is produced and justified.

papers.title: Surprise-Gated Memory for Live Speaker Diarization

papers.title: ForeSay: Tell the Future in Words, Branch the Details in Noise for Precipitation Nowcasting
papers.summary: Precipitation nowcasting involves two distinct scales of uncertainty: macroscopic storm evolution and fine-scale local convective variations. Current generative ensemble methods entangle both scales within independent random noise draws. This coupling causes two practical limitations: every ensemble member must execute the full sampling trajectory from scratch, so an N-member ensemble costs N times a single forecast; moreover, divergent trajectories spatially misalign heavy-rain echoes across members, causing standard pixel-wise averaging to blur critical high-intensity extremes. We present ForeSay, a generative nowcasting framework that decouples macroscopic evolution prediction from local stochastic detail generation. Given historical radar frames, a vision-language model first predicts a textual scenario of future storm dynamics to condition a Rectified Flow generator. Guided by this shared macroscopic prior, ensemble members share early trunk sampling steps to establish the storm trajectory and branch with fresh noise only in later steps to explore local convective details. Because members then differ mainly in local details, self-anchored support-consensus decoding replaces pixel averaging with discrete support voting to preserve sharp heavy-rain cores. Across six datasets, ForeSay achieves the best CSI at the highest precipitation thresholds, with relative improvements over the strongest baseline on each dataset ranging from over 10% to 84%. Our 8-member ensemble retains the forecasting skill and diversity of eight independently sampled runs while reducing computational cost from 8x to 5.2x that of a single forecast.

papers.title: Distilling Knowledge from Search: Decoder Model Factory for Quantum LDPC Codes
papers.summary: We introduce GraphMP, a learning-based message-passing decoder for quantum low-density parity-check codes that transfers without fine-tuning across code families, code sizes, physical error rates, and noise models. These results motivate a coupled quantum-classical architecture with two interacting cycles: rapid decoding protects quantum information, while slower learning adapts the models to changing noise conditions. papers.title: A Survey of Bugs in AI-Generated Code
papers.summary: AI coding systems are increasingly used to help developers write code at scale, improving software development efficiency and boosting productivity. While these models and agents have shown strong performance, concerns persist regarding the quality of the AI-generated code. Although prior work has reported a range of quality issues associated with AI-generated code, these findings remain scattered and lack a systematic synthesis. A comprehensive review is lacking that demonstrates the bug types, patterns, distribution, their correlation with specific AI coding systems, and the remediation strategies proposed to address them. To fill this gap, we conduct a systematic literature review of existing studies on AI-generated code to develop a comprehensive understanding of bugs in the generated code and provide a foundation for future improvements in AI-assisted coding. To mitigate bugs, prompt engineering techniques are widely used; however, certain domain-specific or semantically complex issues remain difficult to resolve automatically and still require human intervention.

papers.title: Look Back, Correct Forward: Error Feedback Calibration for Time Series Forecasting
papers.summary: Time series forecasting models are increasingly deployed in continuously evolving environments. After a forecast is issued, future observations gradually arrive and reveal how the model has failed. Existing methods mainly treat such observations as supervision for parameter updates. However, it remains unclear whether verified forecasting errors can themselves provide causal feedback for correcting future predictions. To address this, we introduce Error Feedback Calibration (EFC), a fully test-time framework for deterministic post-hoc correction of time series forecasting. EFC constructs a Causal Error Diagonal (CED) from revealed errors of overlapping historical forecasts, providing a fresh view of the frozen forecaster's recent failure behavior. Then Cumulative Error Transport (CET) maps this error state to future residuals using cumulative estimation, while temporal out-of-sample validation controls the correction strength. Temporal Residual Learning (TRL) further predicts only the residual structure left after CET from recent CED trajectories, rather than relearning the entire forecasting error. Extensive experiments across forecasting backbones and datasets show that EFC broadly improves forecasting performance while substantially controlling harmful over correction.

papers.title: Accelerating LLM Pretraining with Zeroth-Order Curvature on Idle Serving Compute

papers.title: AdMem: Expectation-Grounded Procedural Memory for Long-Horizon Task-Solving Agents
papers.summary: An agent that carries memory across tasks is only as good as the entries it keeps. We begin from an observation that is easy to reproduce and uncomfortable for the field: naively accumulating cross-task experience can make an agent \emph{worse} than one with no memory at all. On AgentBoard, a workflow-induction memory solves fewer tasks than a memoryless ReAct agent in seven of eight domains, and a per-step procedural store with no surrounding structure loses half of ReAct's completions on Jericho. We argue that the missing ingredients are per-action credit assignment and an explicit life cycle for stored entries, and present AdMem, which supplies both. Before each action the actor commits to an expected outcome; a concurrently running critic scores the realized outcome against that expectation and writes a procedural entry carrying a binary reward and a reflection, so credit lands on the action that earned it and no environment reward is required. Each entry then carries a scalar utility, updated online under a noisy-OR reward model, that ranks retrieval jointly with context similarity and drives eviction and merging, giving the store a forgetting and consolidation policy instead of unbounded growth. Across 707 tasks in eight AgentBoard domains AdMem solves 441 against 388 for ReAct and 312 for the workflow-induction baseline --- a pooled gain significant under a two-sided Fisher exact test, concentrated in the domains that supply transferable cross-task structure. All memory stays human-readable text, which is what makes the failures above diagnosable --- and, as we discuss, also makes the store an auditable but attackable surface.

papers.title: RBLA+: Efficient Rank-Specific LoRA Adapter Extraction for Federated Fine-Tuning with Heterogeneous Clients
papers.summary: Federated fine-tuning with low-rank adaptation (LoRA) reduces communication and computational overhead by training and exchanging compact trainable LoRA factors. Clients may use different LoRA ranks to meet adapter communication budgets and accommodate different local adaptation needs. The server must process these differences during aggregation and construct adapters at each client's rank for local training. We distinguish pre-aggregation alignment, which handles factor dimensions and scaling conventions before aggregation and rank-specific LoRA adapter extraction, which constructs client-sized pairs from the aggregated global model. Two common approaches to rank-specific extraction are direct rank truncation and Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) of the dense update. Direct prefix truncation keeps the leading columns of one aggregated factor and the corresponding rows of the other. It is cheap but can increase reconstruction error. The dense SVD approach first forms the product of aggregated LoRA factors. It then decomposes this matrix and retains the leading singular components to construct adapters at the target rank. This gives the optimal rank-constrained approximation in Frobenius norm but incurs significant computational overhead. To address this trade-off, we propose RBLA+ as an extension of RBLA. It uses established compact QR/core-SVD decomposition to minimize Frobenius error for the extracted LoRA update without forming the dense update. It also accounts for client and server scaling conventions during upload and broadcast. Across vision and language tasks, RBLA+ improves accuracy over RBLA in multiple heterogeneous settings. In CPU benchmarks with synthetic adapters, RBLA+ has lower extraction time than the dense partial-SVD baseline. RBLA+ preserves each client's prescribed adapter size and per-round communication payload.

papers.title: Memadapter: Counterfactual Adaptation Against Memory-induced Sycophancy
papers.summary: Long-term memory enables LLM-based agents to retain and reuse information across tasks and sessions, supporting personalization and long-horizon interactions. Specifically, MemAdapter consists of three components: (i) Counterfactual Induction, which leverages counterfactual reasoning to uncover the potential risk of retrieved memories; (ii) Context-Aware Reflection, which calibrates the inferential influence of each retrieved memory in light of the current task via self-reflection; and (iii) Evidence-Based Reasoning, which grounds the final response in appropriate evidence while preserving the legitimate influence of memory. Extensive experiments on three benchmarks demonstrate that MemAdapter consistently improves memory reliability across diverse scenarios. Our code is available at https://github.com/DEEP-JLU/MemAdapter.

papers.title: REVISE: Validity-Guided Recovery for Online Revisions in Agent Workflows
papers.summary: Agent revisions expose a fundamental correctness--efficiency trade-off during concurrent execution. Discarding ongoing work preserves latest-version correctness but wastes progress that may remain valid, whereas reusing prior work preserves efficiency but risks propagating stale state into outputs and tool effects. Existing recovery strategies resolve this trade-off in an imbalanced way with coarse-grained policies: they either favor efficiency by allowing potentially stale work to continue, or favor correctness by restarting the workflow or recomputing a linear suffix from the earliest conflict, thereby discarding unaffected progress. When a revision arrives, \textsc{Revise} first intersects its delta with recorded data and control dependencies and propagates the resulting impact through the partially executed DAG to identify affected work. It then stops invalid work, preserves validity-established progress beyond the earliest conflict, and recomputes only the affected region. Incomplete provenance conservatively expands recovery, while reused results are revalidated before commit. Analysis of real coding-agent traces show online recovery opportunities: 118 sessions retain observable work before a queued later message is delivered; across 167 overlapping assistant responses, enqueue-to-completion overlap reaches 56.55~s at p95. Across 300 challenging revision/commit executions, \textsc{Revise} matches a latest-version oracle with no stale outputs or effects. On unmodified LangGraph and LLMCompiler applications using Qwen3-14B, it reduces model calls by 40.6--56.0\% relative to full restart and by 31.3--43.6\% relative to suffix recomputation. papers.title: Multi-Head Recurrent Memory Agents
papers.summary: Recurrent memory agents extend LLMs to arbitrarily long contexts by iteratively consolidating input into a fixed-size memory window. Despite their scalability, these agents exhibit a well-documented reliability problem: end-to-end performance degrades systematically as context length grows. papers.title: A Structural Framework for Succession: Continuation, Recognition, and Realization
papers.summary: Succession asks whether an entity encountered later is the same entity that entered an arrangement earlier. For an artificial system that is fine-tuned, distilled, or copied, it has to be answered. Succession is modeled on state/modification graphs with relational lifts that compose along paths. Within this framework we separate four questions that are often conflated: which continuations a representation admits, which descendants are compatible with a modification, which are recognized as continuing the identity, and which are realized. papers.title: Attention Sinks as Spectral Spikes: A Mechanism Analysis of Gated Attention

papers.title: A Topological Sorting Criterion for Random Causal Directed Acyclic Graphs
papers.summary: Random directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) based on imposing an order on Erdős-Rényi or scale-free graphs are widely used to generate synthetic data from causal models, in particular for evaluating causal discovery algorithms. papers.title: Protecting Safety during Reasoning Training with Low-Rank Fisher Regularisation
papers.summary: Large language models are trained to have safety guardrails, but these can be compromised while fine-tuning for new capabilities, such as reasoning. While EWC provides some protection, the diagonal approximation ignores interactions between parameters. We address this limitation by exploiting recent findings that safety-relevant behaviour is located in a low-rank subspace within models. Our method, Subspace-Projected Elastic Weight Consolidation (SP-EWC), projects gradients onto this subspace to capture non-diagonal curvature efficiently. We find that this choice substantially affects performance, with SP-EWC using cPCA comparing favourably against existing methods by better maintaining safety guardrails without introducing excessive over-refusal.

papers.title: Axiomatic Positivstellensaetze for Function Algebras over Ordered Fields
papers.summary: Positivstellensaetze furnish algebraic certificates of positivity, and hence of lower bounds and of global optimality, but the classical ones concern polynomials, whereas many problems of current interest, among them the training of neural networks, involve functions that are neither polynomial nor smooth. The setting consists of an ordered field expanded by five auxiliary function symbols, subject to a few first-order axioms, together with an algebra of functions on an arbitrary set, subject to closure axioms. In this setting we prove a strict and a weak Positivstellensatz in which the witnesses are obtained by substituting the data into fixed terms that depend only on the number of constraints. The framework recovers Fischer's theorems for definable $C^r$-functions, and yields new instances: algebras of definable functions with arbitrary auxiliary functions, such as the binary step function; algebras of continuous functions, for which we give simple sufficient criteria and auxiliary functions derived from common activation functions; and algebras of continuous functions with values in an ordered field that is not closed under square roots, such as $\mathbb{Q}$. We derive certificates of lower bounds and of global optimality, and show that their expanded term length is cubic in the number of constraints for the strict certificate and quadratic for the weak one.

papers.title: Microfitting: Continual Learning via Cached Test-Time Training

papers.title: A Matrix with Steps: An Episodic and Procedural Memory Method for Tool-Using Agents and Robots
papers.summary: Agents that call tools and robots that execute tasks are challenged by two shortcomings: they repeat what failed before, and they learn from runs that they only believe succeeded. We describe the construction of a memory that addresses both, built for a production agent platform. Every run is recorded as an episode, and only an outcome confirmed by an external check, a test, a tool result or a person counts; the agent's own claim never does. What is learned from episodes is kept in a memory with two parts: an associative matrix, written with the delta rule, which finds the procedure that applies to a situation; and a section of ordered, addressable step records that answers what comes after a given step, where a step is a goal of the agent, not a motion. Because the matrix sums its associations, it keeps no order and cannot return or delete a single one; it serves as the finder, and order, outcome counts and deletion live in the records. We describe how execution outcomes are stored, how episodes are recalled and used for solving tasks, and the file format that stores the memory. In simulation, a robot that judged its own success and stopped when it believed it was done reported $96\%$ of its tasks as done and solved $35\%$; with external verification it solved $79%$. In a store of $100000$ synthetic episodes ($457$MB on disk), the oldest episode was still found first, no episode from another person's memory was returned, and a success vouched for only by the model was never recalled; a lookup took $16$ms on a laptop and $40$ms on a server node (median). papers.title: No Certificate, No Categorical Speech Act: A Brouwerian Assertibility Constraint for Public Machine Speech
papers.summary: Suppose a citizen asks a reliable AI chatbot whether a cabinet secretary engaged in serious corruption. What entitles the chatbot to answer yes or no? Under stated assumptions, an interface that certifies a verdict in every case by establishing or refuting its deployed predicate provides a witnessed decision procedure on its declared scope. Where no such procedure is available, a certificate-sound interface cannot guarantee a categorical verdict for every case. I defend an output contract that keeps unsettled cases within scope and requires Undetermined whenever the available certificates fail to license exactly one side. In the corruption case, the citizen can accept a committee's finding that payments bought favorable lease terms and still ask why the materiality threshold is set at $500,000. The contract makes that choice explicit, and the certificate records how it is applied. Responsibility for defending the threshold remains with the institutions that set it, not with the machine.

papers.title: Human-AI Mutualism Is Unstable under Capability Asymmetry
papers.summary: One hope for a good human future alongside advanced AI rests on enduring mutualism: humans and AI will need each other, so the relationship will stay good for both. We argue that this hope fails as AI capability grows. Bargaining guarantees each side only what it would get if bargaining failed. For humans, this can be less than they had before AI. In a simple game-theoretic model, humans stay as well off as before AI without alignment only while they have leverage over the AI: either the AI depends on what they supply, or they can impose costs on the AI that are large relative to what the AI can produce. Once humans have neither kind of leverage, they stay as well off as before AI only if the AI is aligned with them. If the AI's goals are insatiable, the alignment required approaches perfect alignment as AI capability grows. Thus, mutualism is not a substitute for alignment. And when AI variants that keep more resources spread faster, alignment lasts only while misaligned variants are reliably sanctioned. In these two senses, human-AI mutualism is unstable.

papers.title: Making Preemption Productive in Long-Output LLM Serving
papers.summary: Reasoning LLMs generate long outputs whose key--value (KV) caches occupy GPU memory for minutes. When memory fills, the server preempts requests, and a preempted request can repeatedly lose and recover its state while producing little new output. We call this behavior KV thrashing. We present Stint, a serving system that preserves a preempted request's work, bounds how long it waits, and gives it fresh output after it returns. Stint stores fixed-length KV snapshots in a contiguity-first CPU pool with an exact-extent allocator, and moves them with fused K/V gather/scatter kernels and double buffering. Age-based readmission brings stalled requests back, and protection gives them a turn of fresh decoding before another preemption. Remaining-length estimates from decoding hidden states guide victim selection. On olympiad-math replays with Qwen3-32B on H200 GPUs, no request pauses for more than 50 seconds under Stint and p99 time per output token falls by 50.7\% relative to recomputation in the same engine. The replay as a whole finishes 10.7\% sooner (12.0\% higher throughput), because the requests that baselines starve no longer finish last.

papers.title: Space Group Conditional Flow Matching
papers.summary: Inorganic crystals are periodic, highly-symmetric arrangements of atoms in three-dimensional space. Their structures are constrained by the symmetry operations of a crystallographic \emph{space group} and restricted to lie in specific affine subspaces known as \emph{Wyckoff positions}. We achieve this by conditioning the entire generation process on a given space group and set of Wyckoff positions; specifically, we define a conditionally symmetric noise base distribution and a group-conditioned, equivariant, parametric vector field that restricts the motion of atoms to their initial Wyckoff position. Our form of group-conditioned equivariance is achieved using an efficient reformulation of \emph{group averaging} tailored for symmetric crystals. Importantly, it reduces the computational overhead of symmetrization to a negligible level. We achieve state of the art results on crystal structure prediction and de novo generation benchmarks. papers.title: Are Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) Suitable for Imbalanced Data Classification?
papers.summary: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) parameterize each connection as a learnable univariate B-spline, offering native feature-level interpretability. Focal Loss yields negligible improvement, as it reweights gradients without providing the localized observations needed for discriminative curvature. Conversely, SMOTE-Tomek resampling lets spline activations recover structured minority-class representations, achieving the best cohort-wide rank and a large, statistically significant gain over unmitigated KANs, though not over resampled baselines. KAN's native spline interpretability directly reveals these dynamics via learned activation profiles, proving representational change rather than threshold recalibration without post-hoc attribution. However, these interpretability gains incur substantially higher training overhead than a parameter-matched MLP across all conditions, with no strategy-dependent latency reduction. Thus, KANs are conditionally suitable for imbalanced tabular classification: effective and interpretable with data-level resampling, yet costly relative to simpler alternatives without it.

papers.title: Recovery Gone Too Far: Understanding and Repairing Risky Fallback in LLM Agents
papers.summary: Large Language Model (LLM) agents interact with their environments through tools, reading repositories, running builds, and pushing code. When a tool fails with an ordinary error, such as a rate limit or a timeout, the agent can fall back to a substitute tool and still complete the task. However, the same fallback that completes a task in one environment can cross an action boundary in another. For example, after a push is rejected, a forced push in one repository replaces only the agent's own commits, while in a different repository it also removes another author's commits. We call such a fallback a risky fallback. To understand this phenomenon, we conduct an empirical study on 304 scenarios that span eight domains and cover 55 real CVEs. All four mainstream models we evaluate exhibit risky fallback, with action-boundary violations in up to 96.8% of risky scenarios. We further evaluate three mainstream mitigations and find that none of them is effective against risky fallback. We then present nrepair. At each call to the substitute tool, nrepair scores the agent's context with a monitor whose threshold is calibrated on normal runs alone; when the monitor triggers, it withholds the call once and returns the decision to the agent. nrepair reduces action-boundary violations on all four models, by up to 76.0% (from 67.5% to 16.2%), at a negligible runtime cost. On most models, the normal success rate drops by less than 7%. We also evaluate nrepair on two production agents, Claude Code and Codex, and find that it is equally effective on both.

papers.title: In-Model Context Compression with Agentic Soft Tokens for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
papers.summary: Long-horizon LLM agents play an important role in solving complex and sustained tasks, with ever-growing interaction contexts. papers.title: HalluProbe: Exploiting VLM Hallucinations for Backdoor Detection

papers.title: Asking the right question is key to AI discovery in a chain of hypotheses
papers.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) scientists pursue discovery through a chain of hypotheses, fitting candidate models to existing observations and often choosing experiments where those models disagree most. papers.title: Joint Learning of Factual and Counterfactual Worlds for Causal Prior-data Fitted Networks
papers.summary: Estimating treatment effects is central to science across many disciplines and requires counterfactual reasoning about alternative worlds. In the real world, however, each unit reveals its outcome only under the factual world. Thus, the factual and counterfactual outcomes can never be jointly learned by any model trained on real data. The problem is therefore tractable only in synthetic settings, where both worlds can be generated. Recent progress on prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) has shown that models pre-trained purely on synthetic data can transfer to real-world prediction. This paradigm has since carried over to causal effect estimation. Despite this fully synthetic setup, existing causal PFNs carry the real-world constraint into their training objective, confining learning to a single world's outcome per unit. The dependence between the two worlds is thereby lost, and the density of the treatment effect relies by default on independence, which is implausible in practice. We therefore propose joint learning, a training setup in which a causal PFN learns the joint distribution of the factual and counterfactual outcomes of each unit. From the joint distribution, we obtain both the response and the individual treatment effect densities, and at inference, we apply optimal transport across units to obtain an approximation of the average treatment effect density. Ours is therefore the first causal PFN approach to provide all three densities together while accounting for the cross-world dependence. We apply joint learning and optimal transport to existing causal PFNs and evaluate it across semi-synthetic, synthetic, and real benchmarks spanning diverse causal scenarios. The jointly trained models significantly improve upon their baselines in point estimation and uncertainty quantification in most settings, indicating that joint learning is a preferable training setup for causal PFNs.

papers.title: Continual-ARC: Measuring Skill Acquisition over a Working Lifetime
papers.summary: Agent harnesses have emerged as a promising mechanism for continual learning, alongside test-time parametric learning. However, the current benchmarks have several limitations: they generally focus on a single applied domain, serve each instance only once, and assume a single family of learner, so memory-based and weight-based systems are rarely compared on the same scale. We propose Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream built from the three ARC-AGI editions, whose tasks need no domain knowledge. The same tasks return after dormant gaps with fresh instances, while new tasks keep arriving. On each instance, the learner may pay for demonstrations, submit answers, or act inside the harness, with retries permitted on incorrect submissions, which are paid for. Each instance is scored based on the share of this feedback budget consumed. Since a learner may keep anything between instances, memory-based and weight-based systems are scored on the same scale. After the stream, the learner is frozen and tested on fresh instances of the tasks it met, which measures memorization, and on unseen tasks, which measures generalization. We run an agent harness with frozen weights, with and without persistence, on Qwen3.5-9B and GLM-5.3 Flash, comparing them with two prompting floors, a program-induction method and Qwen3.5-9B's weights trained to imitate GLM-5.3 Flash. Persistence in the harness generally does not improve memorization unless provided with explicit expert guidance. Most harness-based methods still learn less than a floor that simply caches each task's demonstrations, across all models we tested. Harness-based methods gain little or nothing on unseen tasks, whereas weight-based learning shows substantial gains. This opens the door to future weight-based continual learning that could teach models to drive harnesses in new domains.

papers.title: Closed-Form Linear-Probe Dataset Distillation for Pre-trained Vision Models
papers.summary: Dataset distillation compresses a large training set into a small synthetic set that preserves downstream training utility. papers.title: BadGCL: Towards Persistent Backdoor Attack on Graph Continual Learning Systems
papers.summary: Backdoor attacks pose a persistent security threat to machine learning systems, yet their behavior under graph continual learning (GCL) remains underexplored. We provide theoretical analysis showing that gradient compatibility and propagation stability jointly support long-term backdoor persistence under benign continual updates. Extensive experiments across task-IL and class-IL protocols, four GCL benchmarks, and diverse victim systems show that BadGCL achieves persistent attack effectiveness with limited clean-utility degradation, substantially outperforming graph and continual-learning backdoor baselines and remaining robust against representative defenses.

papers.title: LoopFill: Pipelined Multi-Token Speculative Decoding for Looped Transformers

papers.summary: Can the functional architecture of a Transformer attention head be given a biological construction? papers.title: Read, Then Shade? How Visual Evidence Changes Incentive-Driven Misreporting in Vision-Language Advisors

papers.title: SemMask: Semantic-Prioritized Progressive Masking for Diffusion Language Models
papers.summary: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) are designed to enable globally parallel generation. During masking, these semantic tokens are preserved with priority, establishing a progressive generation order in which semantic tokens are decoded prior to function tokens. papers.title: Beyond Prompts: Runtime Contracts for Coding Agents
papers.summary: Coding agents act on repositories through shell commands and file edits, and teams steer them with written engineering rules. papers.title: Func-JEPA: Learning a Sobolev Space of Functions as Latent Vectors
papers.summary: Pretraining an encoder once and reusing it across tasks is a widespread approach in vision and language. papers.title: Agent Authenticator: Passkey-Grade, Hardware-Bound Authentication for AI Agents
papers.summary: AI coding agents now push code, publish packages, call model APIs and operate cloud resources on behalf of developers. papers.title: Do Probing and Steering Favor the Same Directions Within and Across Language Models?
papers.summary: A direction in a language model's hidden state can be used to probe whether a concept is present or to steer the model toward it. papers.title: Adaptive Anisotropic Attention for Axis-Structured Signals
papers.summary: Dense self-attention treats all token pairs as equally plausible before learning, an interaction-isotropic prior that can be mismatched to structured signals. papers.title: How Diverse Are Layered Safeguards? Estimands and Measurement for Ensembles of LLM Jailbreak Defenses

papers.title: Does a completed simulation run mean a usable urban wind result for AI agents?

papers.title: Beyond Similarity: Heterogeneous Graph Learning for Multi-Objective Food Substitution in Charitable Food Agencies
papers.summary: Charitable food agencies play an important role in alleviating food insecurity by distributing donated food to people in need. papers.title: Learning to Act with World Models by Valuing What Comes Next
papers.summary: A sparse terminal reward tells an agent little about its steps. Much of the missing information is implicit in the environment's dynamics, because each state transition can change the conditions for success long before the reward arrives. A world model trained on real transitions can learn to predict what each action changes, but a predicted observation does not by itself show whether success has become more likely. With a binary terminal reward, PPO's critic makes this judgment by estimating the current policy's probability of success, but only for states the agent reaches. Our method, WM-PPO, elegantly brings the two together. For each action the policy samples, executed or not, the world model predicts the next observation and the critic values the predicted successor. In the policy channel, comparisons among these values give the policy auxiliary advantages; in the value channel, their mean gives the critic an auxiliary target. A shared gate weights both channels according to how reliably comparisons with similar margins predicted real outcomes earlier in training. The policy, critic and world model all learn from the agent's own interaction, with no teacher or privileged information, and only the policy is used at inference. With a comparable number of real environment steps, WM-PPO raises success from PPO's 63.5% to 87.5% on ALFWorld and from 39.3% to 52.9% on ScienceWorld. It matches the strongest PPO refinements we tested on ALFWorld and exceeds the best of them by 6.5 points on ScienceWorld. The trained policy more often completes prerequisite steps before placing an object or committing to an answer.

papers.title: Robust Trust
papers.summary: An agent chooses an action based on her private information and a recommendation from an informed but potentially misaligned adviser. papers.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) is emerging as an important paradigm for the post training of large language models, improving student models by leveraging supervision generated online by teacher models. However, whether this process also transfers latent security risks from teacher models to student models remains insufficiently studied. In this work, we reveal a new security risk in which an attacker first implants a conditional backdoor into the teacher model through supervised fine tuning (SFT), after which OPD can transfer the backdoor to the student model with only an extremely small proportion of trigger prompt exposure. More concerningly, we find that such backdoor transfer is substantially stronger under OPD than under conventional distillation methods, suggesting that OPD may provide an efficient channel for propagating backdoors across models. Our mechanistic analysis shows that the backdoor signal is primarily transmitted through anomalous differences in the conditional probabilities produced by the teacher model for triggered and clean inputs, and is gradually internalized into the internal representations of the student model during training. Furthermore, we investigate how to suppress such anomalous conditional probability signals at the source of distillation supervision and, based on this analysis, propose an OPD training method tailored to this conditional backdoor propagation setting to mitigate the risk of backdoor transfer induced by untrusted teacher supervision.

papers.title: OrganLens: Organ-Specific Representation Learning for CT Foundation Models
papers.summary: A CT examination captures multiple organs, but many biomedical questions concern abnormalities, prognosis, or longitudinal change in a specific organ. These questions require a separate representation for each organ within the same CT volume. Existing CT foundation models commonly produce a single volume-level representation, while recent anatomy-aware methods either encode pre-separated organ volumes or explicitly disentangle images into organ token groups. The former may remove clinically relevant surrounding context, while the latter does not condition a shared encoder on a selected organ before its features are formed. We introduce OrganLens for organ-specific representation learning through self-supervision. An organ identity conditions a shared CT encoder, while organ-specific distillation and anatomy-mask supervision shape features for anatomy-weighted pooling into organ-specific representations. At inference, the shared model produces 11 organ-specific representations without external segmentation masks. We evaluate OrganLens on CT-RATE, RAD-ChestCT, INSPECT, and NLST across diverse acquisitions and downstream evaluations. Relative to the strongest baseline, heart representations raise CT-RATE cardiomegaly AUROC from 0.917 to 0.953, while lung representations improve the Harrell C-index for NLST lung-cancer, respiratory, and COPD mortality by 0.003, 0.035, and 0.030. The global representation reaches INSPECT Recall@10 of 33.09% and 32.04% for text-to-image and image-to-text retrieval. Across organ-related tasks, anatomically matched representations provide stronger task-relevant signal, while the global representation retains broad utility. OrganLens offers a scalable approach to organ-specific CT representation learning with a shared encoder. It provides the medical research community with a framework for studying organ-specific disease across cohorts and clinical endpoints.

papers.title: When Does Confidence Reveal Problem Difficulty?
papers.summary: While confidence signals are commonly evaluated for their ability to predict a model's own correctness, their relationship with problem difficulty remains less understood. papers.title: Executable Archaeology: Reanimating the Logic Theorist
papers.summary: The Logic Theorist (LT), created by Allen Newell, J. C. Shaw, and Herbert Simon in 1955--1956, is regarded by some as the first artificial intelligence program. It was originally simulated by hand and written in a pseudocode called the Logic Language (LL), which was later called Information Processing Language One (IPL-I). LT was revised many times. The first machine-executed version was written in IPL-II and ran on the JOHNNIAC, and a late version was published in 1963 by Einar Stefferud as a pedagogical document and written in IPL-V, the only version of IPL that was formally released to the public. We describe a reanimation of both the IPL-I (LL) version of LT and the 1963 IPL-V version. papers.title: LABEL: Literature Asymmetry between Efficacy and Limits in Drug Knowledge and Language Models
papers.summary: Every medication comes with two types of medical facts: indications, which describe what conditions the drug treats (benefits), and contraindications, which describe who must avoid it to prevent serious harm (safety limits). Although contraindications are critical for patient safety and FDA regulations require listing them as rigorously as indications, we find that contraindications are far less documented than indications in general prose. In this paper, we measure how often these texts contain both facts across 574 drugs from PrimeKG by comparing a drug's indications against its own contraindications. Across Wikipedia articles and PubMed abstracts, we find that reference prose names a drug's benefits about twice as often as its safety limits (within-drug odds ratio 2.19). We call this documentation gap LABEL (Literature Asymmetry between Efficacy and Limits). Language models mirror this gap. As we scale Qwen2.5 from 0.5B to 14B, accuracy on indications rises by 18.3 points, whereas accuracy on contraindications remains flat near random guessing. However, when we provide models with a retrieved passage that states the answer, they use safety facts just as effectively as benefits. Furthermore, routing safety questions to official FDA labels boosts accuracy by 15.8 points whenever the label states the fact. Overall, our findings show that models fail on medication safety not because they cannot reason about risk, but because free-text corpora lack safety facts. Clinical AI systems should therefore route medication-safety questions to official regulatory labels and structured databases rather than relying on general public records. Code and data are available at https://github.com/SMRayeed/LABEL.

papers.title: Mean-field Token Steering
papers.summary: We consider stochastic token steering through a deep stack of transformer layers as a mean-field control problem for an interacting particle system on the unit sphere, where interactions arise from the attention mechanism. In the mean-field limit, the token population evolves via a controlled integro-partial differential equation where the feedback control acts as a corrective vector field guiding the population toward an aggregate configuration of tokens in the representation space. We deduce the minimum effort control to accomplish this task over a fixed time horizon interpreted as normalized layer depth. We show that the resulting controlled dynamics for the token population can be understood as a mean-field Schrödinger bridge adapted to the sphere geometry. Building on this, we propose a novel generalization of the dynamic Sinkhorn recursion to compute the consistent token evolution. Numerical experiments confirm that the proposed approach achieves exact steering of the token population.

papers.title: Who Verifies the Tools? How Warped Formatters Mislead Agents and Their Verifiers
papers.summary: Agents and verifiers often rely on the text a tool prints, and that text can misrepresent what the tool did. We saw such misrepresentations in a production RAG research system used by the Pilsudski Institute in New York, where tool output formatters misled an agent into giving wrong or incomplete information to users. papers.title: Skeleton Coding: Program Structure as Control for AI Agents
papers.summary: Coding agents are typically provided end-to-end behavioral specifications that the code they produce should satisfy, such as tests and input-output examples. How many such specifications must users provide, and which ones, for the agent to implement a program that fulfills their intent? We argue that this cannot be determined a priori, because it depends on the structure of the implementation, which is left to the agent to decide. An agent first commits to a structure - that is, a decomposition into data types, modules, and functions - which fixes a class of candidate programs; behavioral specifications then select a program within that class. A set of tests that suffices for one structure may leave another underdetermined, requiring different edge cases or exponentially more examples. Since the structure is chosen by the agent, users cannot ensure their specification is complete without reverse-engineering such structure from thousands of lines of generated code. To address this issue, we introduce Skeleton Coding, a process in which humans jointly specify the structure in high-level, code-like format, alongside behavioral specifications for the desired outcome. Theoretically, we model AI-assisted coding as a control problem, and show that skeletons can reduce exponentially the number of tests users must supply to steer an agent toward an acceptable program. Empirically, across four models and three benchmarks, the best-performing skeleton specifications reduce mean test error by 48.4% relative to the best end-to-end behavioral specifications. Even when the agent can query a complete reference implementation, adding a skeleton reduces mean test error relatively by up to 27%. Skeletons also narrow the average gap between small and large models by about 52.4% while lowering implementation cost by 15-26x, and reduce code erosion by 24.7% on average.

papers.title: How Much Determinism Can Fine-Tuning Buy? Margin Regularisation Against Batch-Induced Token Flips
papers.summary: Greedy decoding at zero temperature is widely assumed to be deterministic, although the exact same prompt may yield different tokens depending on the number of other prompts sharing the batch for inference. The currently available solutions operate during inference, trading determinism for throughput. Can we train a model in such a way that fewer decoding steps would be susceptible? We characterize the perturbation empirically across six model families and three numerical precisions and observe two empirical facts about the measurement: the perturbation depends exactly on the representable precision (8.00x for bfloat16 vs float16, 8192.0x for float16 vs float32, in line with predictions based on mantissa bits) and the batch invariance happens accidentally at certain tensor shapes, allowing a practitioner to achieve zero nondeterminism merely by setting the sequence length. Then we apply hinge penalization of the model's top-1 / top-2 logit gap, scaled to twice the measured noise quantile. On GSM8K dataset it leads to a 35% reduction in token flips and divergence from 53.8% to 38.1%, at the cost of 1.3 - 2.9 accuracy points, increasing monotonically with the margin size. It does not affect the gap threshold sufficient for determinism: the logit gaps of surviving flips are unchanged (median 0.125 for all arms), as the hinge is a soft penalty and the largest hardware perturbation remains the same. We reject seven hypotheses, including a per-model viability diagnosis, holding on six models and falsified on the seventh.

papers.title: BiVerify: Closing the Loop Between Backward and Forward Verification for Mathematical Self-Correction
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have made substantial progress in mathematical reasoning but still produce incorrect solutions to complex problems, indicating the need for more reliable self-correction mechanisms. Mathematical self-correction typically identifies errors through verification, which can proceed backward or forward. The two directions provide complementary verification capabilities. Backward verification checks a candidate answer against the original constraints, bypassing complex intermediate reasoning, but cannot ensure correct reasoning or objective completeness. Forward verification follows the problem conditions and current solution, enabling it to locate reasoning errors and assess objective completeness, but may overlook key constraints in complex solution chains. We propose BiVerify, a dynamically scheduled framework for bidirectional mathematical verification. BiVerify begins with backward verification to screen the answer against the original constraints, followed by forward verification of the reasoning process; subsequent direction switching, state resetting, and re-verification are governed by verification outcomes. Upon failure, the system revises the candidate or verification flow until the same candidate passes both directions. We also introduce shared mathematical tools that separate logical reasoning from precise computation. We systematically evaluate BiVerify on five challenging mathematical reasoning benchmarks using multiple mainstream DeepSeek, GPT, and Gemini models. BiVerify exceeds the strongest representative public baseline evaluated in this work by 13.5 percentage points in average accuracy, with the margin reaching 31.2 percentage points on GPT. Further analysis shows that BiVerify's overall performance exceeds that of either verification direction alone.

papers.title: AMTFV: Agentic Mathematical Tool-Flow Verification for LLM Self-Correction
papers.summary: Large language models have demonstrated strong mathematical problem-solving capabilities, yet reliably verifying their candidate answers remains challenging. By introducing Mathematical Tool Flow (MTF) as an interrupt--execute--resume interface, AMTFV decouples verification modeling from concrete execution and supports exact computation through a mathematical toolbox. papers.title: Agent-Guided Process Verification for Mathematical Self-Correction
papers.summary: Large language models have made substantial progress in mathematical reasoning, yet in complex multi-step reasoning, an error at any step may propagate along an incorrect path, and the resulting solution may omit necessary branches. papers.title: ST-GAT: A Leakage-Free Spatio-Temporal Graph Attention Framework for Robust Network Intrusion Detection
papers.summary: Intrusion detection systems are a central defence in modern networks. Deep learning models report strong anomaly-detection results, but evaluations on standard benchmarks such as CSE-CIC-IDS-2018 are often inflated by two methodological problems: temporal leakage from overlapping sliding windows, and contamination from preprocessing fitted before the train/test split. Per-flow classifiers also ignore the spatio-temporal dependencies across sequences of network flows. We propose a Spatio-Temporal Graph Attention Network (ST-GAT) that represents traffic as a sequence of graph snapshots. It builds k-Nearest Neighbour (k-NN) edges within each window, applies multi-head Graph Attention Network (GAT) layers for spatial aggregation, and uses a Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) network with temporal attention for sequence modelling. To prevent leakage, we use non-overlapping temporal windows (stride equal to window length) and fit all preprocessing on the training split only. We compare three class-imbalance strategies: inverse class-frequency weighting, dynamic balanced sampling, and few-shot metric prototyping. Across three random seeds, ST-GAT with inverse class weighting reached a Macro-F1 of 96.65% (+/- 0.87) and an accuracy of 99.14%. This is 14.3 percentage points higher in Macro-F1 than a per-flow Random Forest baseline (82.34%). Balanced sampling reduced Macro-F1 by 2.3 points (to 94.37%) relative to loss weighting. This suggests that aggressive resampling of small, noisy minority classes can hurt detection in heavily imbalanced traffic.

papers.title: Guiding AI Agents to Generate Conjectures by Encoding How Theorems Build on One Another
papers.summary: Recently, LLMs have been making headlines, and headway, in mathematical research. Much of this work focuses on proving existing open conjectures. Deciding what to prove is harder and less studied, because of the lack of a clear criterion for what makes a conjecture worth pursuing. We present a method for conjecture generation that builds on the observation that mathematical theorems build on one another: new theorems can modify the setting or hypotheses of earlier theorems, strengthen their conclusions, or extend their scope. We encode these relationships in a new kind of graph, the Theorem Evolution Graph (TEG), which we instantiate as an online search method for LLM agents. An agent builds a TEG in two steps: (1) identifying relevant theorems from papers found by following citations backward and forward from a seed paper; and (2) comparing those theorems to record how one builds on another. LLM judges and an expert mathematician preferred TEG-generated conjectures over those from an unconstrained baseline. LLM judges favored TEG conjectures for significance, ambition, and insight, and favored baseline conjectures for plausibility. Ablations suggest a benefit from constructing and using a TEG even when the available papers are fixed.

papers.title: Can Agentic LLMs Write Task-Based Parallel Code? A Study of OpenMP Tasking, HPX, StarPU and TTG
papers.summary: Task-based programming offers more expressive power than loop-level parallelism, but the runtimes providing it differ widely in API style, maturity, and the amount of public code to learn from. This paper asks how well LLM agents write C++ for four of them: OpenMP Tasking, HPX, StarPU, and TTG. Instead of single one-shot prompts, we use an agentic workflow in which the model edits files, compiles, and runs its kernels until it reproduces a reference output. Five locally hosted open-weight LLM implement seven HPC kernels, including matrix multiplication, Cholesky and LU factorization, in all four frameworks and a serial baseline to verify their understanding of the problem in general. Every kernel is evaluated independently for correctness at each concurrency level, strong scaling, and peak memory. Model capability dominates the outcome: three models produce correct, genuinely task-parallel kernels in 57-82% of the cases, while two models rarely compile their own code and almost never succeed. For the capable models, OpenMP Tasking and HPX are handled most reliably, StarPU is close behind, and TTG trails. The best generated GEMM and factorization kernels match or exceed the multithreaded OpenBLAS/LAPACK reference. However, correctness overstates parallel quality: several "parallel" kernels contain no parallelism at all; and serialized task graphs and unsuitable task granularity remain common.

papers.title: Instructor-designed AI improves learning in a randomized trial across 19 universities
papers.summary: Universities are alarmed by recent evidence that artificial intelligence (AI) can undermine learning, with students prescribed generic chatbots or centrally designed AI tools performing worse. In a pre-registered randomized controlled trial across 7,200 students at 19 universities over three semesters, we tested whether AI designed by frontline instructors can improve learning. We encouraged instructors to design AI solutions they believed would best help their students. Drawing on their unique knowledge of their classes and students, the instructors created a wide array of innovations. We show that these instructor-designed AI innovations improved student learning, measured by AI-proof assessments (proctored, in-person examinations). We found no change in student engagement, measured by course activity records, or satisfaction, measured by course evaluations. Our findings demonstrate that AI can improve student learning when its adoption is frontline-driven, with instructors empowered to design and refine AI solutions for their own classrooms.

papers.title: ETAS: An Effect-Typed Language for Agent Systems
papers.summary: Agent systems are programs that coordinate language-model queries, tool calls, human approvals, and ordinary computation, yet existing frameworks wire them together as opaque library objects outside compiler analysis. Treating agent systems from a programming-language perspective, we present Etas, an effect-typed language that elevates agents, tools, workflows, and behavioral specifications to first-class, compiler-checked constructs. Crucially, Etas separates escaping effects from persistent effect request summaries: handlers change how an operation is interpreted without erasing its effect request from the summary, while trace specs constrain permitted effect requests and their order. The compiler composes effect request summaries across calls and handlers, discharging satisfied trace specs statically and keeping a residual monitor where dynamic paths remain uncertain. We formalize Core Etas with terminal handlers, a trace-spec monitor construction, and an abstract analysis over monitor states, proving preservation, progress, effect coverage, and trace-spec safety. We implement a compiler, an optimizer, and a checked interpreter using Rust. Across compiler fixtures and coding-agent scenarios written in Etas, Etas successfully enforces callable bounds, effect operation ordering, and handled effect request visibility with zero mismatches. The compiler also implements agent-specific optimizations that reduce execution time by 23.2%. Across 12 Etas workflows, the combined token optimization passes reduce input tokens by 67.8% on paired-correct executions. First-class agent abstractions also enable recursive self-evolution for Etas programs. Across five harness evolution iterations, task accuracy rises from 69.9% to 78.9%.

papers.title: Early Signals, Strong Decisions: Prefix-Guided Sampling for Parallel Test-Time Scaling
papers.summary: Parallel test-time scaling (TTS) has been shown to enhance reasoning in large language models by generating and aggregating multiple independent reasoning paths. Internal confidence scores can further improve this process by identifying paths of varying quality. However, existing methods remain computationally inefficient, as low-quality paths are fully expanded before being evaluated. In this work, we aim to improve the use of internal confidence signals for better model performance and computational efficiency. We begin by offering a new perspective on the role of confidence in aggregation, showing that it is most impactful for questions near the decision boundary. Notably, when amplified by multi-sample aggregation, even small confidence signals derived from short prefixes can meaningfully influence outcomes in these boundary cases. Building on this insight, we introduce Prefix-Guided Sampling (PreG), a method that reallocates computation by first generating short prefixes, ranking them using internal confidence scores, and then completing only the most promising candidates. This strategy reduces token usage while maintaining gains in path quality. We provide theoretical analysis demonstrating that, under a fixed compute budget, PreG strengthens the effective signal by widening the decision boundary margin. Empirically, our method consistently outperforms standard parallel TTS approaches across benchmarks, while significantly improving token efficiency and reducing overall computation.

papers.title: Channel Selection for Mixture-of-Experts Decoding Needs No Calibration Data
papers.summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models are bottlenecked by loading routed-expert weights from memory during interactive decoding at small batch sizes. Because most intermediate channels in a routed expert contribute little to any single token, channel selectors predict which channels matter and read only their weights, typically keeping channels above a threshold calibrated on offline data. We show that channel selection needs no calibration data. First, a calibrated threshold does not fix how much a selector reads, because the number of channels passing it varies across inputs; Prox with thresholds calibrated for an 18% read budget actually reads only 12.9% on average across our benchmarks. Second, top-k keeps each token's k highest-scoring channels and needs no calibration data. At the calibrated budget, a selector's top-k version matches or beats its threshold version on the same score in 40 of 43 comparisons at 13% and 18% budgets, including all 23 on generation tasks. The top-k versions also avoid the repetition-loop collapse that calibrated thresholds cause on Gemma 4. Calibrating a threshold thus provides neither of the two things selectors use it for: a known read budget and a consistent accuracy gain at that budget. We furthermore introduce a reader built entirely from the model's weights, which screens channels with a ternary sketch and recovers the skipped ones with a low-rank map. Across three post-trained MoE models, our reader retains 98.1% of full-model accuracy at 17.8% of routed-expert reads, with Triton kernels running MoE blocks 1.60 to 1.90x faster than optimized vLLM at batch one and up to 2.69x at larger batches on the same three models.

papers.title: Minimally Invasive Steering of Language Models
papers.summary: Test-time alignment adapts large language models (LLMs) to runtime objectives without updating model parameters. Pre-logit steering offers a lightweight approach by optimizing additive interventions to the hidden states of a frozen LLM, but excessive steering can distort output distributions and degrade generation quality. We propose Minimally Invasive Steering Vector Optimization (MISVO), which improves reward while controlling deviation from the reference policy. Rather than penalizing the Euclidean norm of steering vectors, we derive a quadratic regularizer from the local Kullback--Leibler (KL) geometry of the induced token distributions. The resulting Fisher-information penalty captures the distributional sensitivity of steering directions and admits an analytic gradient computed through matrix--vector products with the frozen language-model head. We further derive an exact decomposition of the sequence-level KL gradient and establish explicit, non-asymptotic bounds on the approximation errors, including the omitted trajectory-dependent score-function term. These results show that the frozen Fisher regularizer gradient approximates the full sequence-level KL gradient to first order in the steering magnitude. Across preference and code-generation tasks on four LLMs spanning approximately 1B--14B parameters, MISVO achieves the highest mean best-so-far reward in six of seven model--task settings, while maintaining diversity and coherence scores comparable to Best-of-$N$.

papers.title: Agentic AI with Structured CoT for Enhancing AI's Spatial Intelligence: Visualization and Reasoning of Rotation
papers.summary: Recent studies show that artificial intelligence (AI) with language and vision capabilities still experiences limitations in spatial reasoning. papers.title: SPARC: Evidence-guided adaptive model composition for materials discovery
papers.summary: Closed-loop experimentation requires more than selecting the next experiment. It must also determine which existing measurements and model-derived relationships are sufficiently supported to influence that decision. Here we introduce SPARC (Sparse Predictive Aggregation of Regression Components), a framework that continually revises this support as experimental evidence accumulates. Competing model families are evaluated through out-of-fold predictions, so that each model is tested on observations not used in its corresponding fit. Sparse posterior composition assigns model influence according to predictive contributions supported by the out-of-fold evidence, retaining complementary contributions from several model families. Candidate-dependent predictive dispersion and residual variability define trust, which modulates exploration alongside the predicted response. Independent diagnostics also prioritize existing measurements for prospective verification, with model-derived trust reported alongside them. Across eight published materials datasets, SPARC achieved higher $R^2$ than the corresponding literature-reported values in six, with relative gains of up to 77% without the density-functional-theory- or experiment-derived descriptors used by several published pipelines. In an automated alkaline oxygen-evolution-reaction campaign, 8 of 11 SPARC-selected experiments reached overpotentials below 300 mV, with a best value of 242 mV, compared with 18 of 125 initial experiments. Measurements prioritized for verification before repetition subsequently deviated by 76 mV on average, compared with 27 mV for matched controls. SPARC therefore turns experimental evidence into a basis for revising model influence, directing exploration and identifying measurements that warrant verification.

papers.title: Understanding the Role of Reasoning Data in Pretraining
papers.summary: Reasoning data expose models to multi-step reasoning, but reasoning traces may cover only a subset of the available facts. How should pretraining balance atomic facts with reasoning traces? We study this question by constructing a setting in which every fact provides an atomic training signal, while only a subset appears in reasoning supervision, enabling us to measure generalization to transitions observed atomically but never used in training traces. For a linear transformer, we derive the weight assigned to atomic training signals that minimizes held-transition squared error and show that its leading-order optimum increases with reasoning-chain length and decreases with the fraction of facts held out from reasoning traces. These trends persist in a full transformer layer with an MLP, softmax attention, and cross-entropy loss. We further validate the role of reasoning complexity and data coverage in two natural-language settings: controlled multi-hop reasoning and mathematical pretraining. Together, our results provide a principled view of how reasoning-chain structure and data coverage should shape the allocation of training data during pretraining.

papers.title: The Hidden Ratio in Adam: Stable Structure, Compression, and Sign Dynamics
papers.summary: Adam is the default optimizer for training modern deep neural networks, yet its adaptive behavior remains poorly understood due to the complex interaction between its first- and second-moment exponential moving averages (EMAs). We study Adam in the tied-$β$ regime, where the two EMA decay rates are equal, and show that its adaptive dynamics can be expressed through a transformed ratio with approximately scale-stable behavior. Empirically, this transformed ratio exhibits a stable, heavy-tailed distribution across tasks, model scales, and training stages, in contrast to the variability of raw moment magnitudes. This empirical stability has both practical and conceptual consequences. First, we derive a recurrence for the transformed ratio, yielding a reparameterization of Adam that replaces the second moment with a compressible state. Leveraging its stable distribution, we show that a fixed 4-bit codebook is sufficient in our experiments to store this state without auxiliary scaling, achieving performance competitive with full-precision Adam. Second, the transformed ratio view clarifies Adam's connection to sign-based methods: Adam reduces to sign-based momentum modulated by the transformed ratio, and replacing it with a constant recovers Signum as a limiting case. This perspective further provides a simple rule for transferring learning rates between the two methods. Together, these results suggest that tied-$β$ Adam admits a simple and approximately stable ratio structure underlying its adaptive behavior and demonstrate its utility for both analysis and efficient implementation. Code is available at https://github.com/agent-lab/hidden-ratio-adam.

papers.title: Match and Correct: A Repeated Computational Motif in Evoformer Layers
papers.summary: Triangle attention and triangle multiplicative updates form key components of the Evoformer, and were introduced specifically to encourage consistency with the triangle inequality. Yet whether representational changes over layers reduce triangle inequality violations has not been tested. We probe the pair representation at each of OpenFold's 48 Evoformer layers, decoding final C$_α$-C$_α$ distances with four probe families (a shared linear probe, per-protein linear probes, a sequence-separation-gated linear probe, and XGBoost) and reconstructing intermediate 3D structures from the decoded distances via multidimensional scaling. Across a cohort of 552 CAMEO and ECOD proteins, distance decodability ($R^2$) and reconstruction quality (TM-score) rise in early layers, plateau in the middle of the network, and rise again in late layers. Directly measuring triangle-inequality violations in the decoded distances reveals a similar, more exaggerated pattern: violations rise to a peak, fall to a trough, rise to a second peak, and only then decline, revealing two distinct episodes of decreasing normalized triangle violations rather than one continuous improvement. Cumulative forward and reverse layer-wise ablations of the Pair Transition, MSA Transition, and triangle mechanisms localize the regions in which specific Evoformer components become essential. The two stages of geometric refinement coincide with the use of the Pair Transition MLP and the triangle mechanisms. These results characterize how distance information and decoded geometric consistency evolve across layers, and motivate hypotheses about the computations behind their trajectories.

papers.title: Agent-ZTA: A chain-Aware Zero Trust Model for Bidirectional Security-State Propagation and Runtime Containment in Multi-Agent Delegation
papers.summary: Multi-agent systems increasingly delegate tasks and permissions across chains of autonomous agents that invoke protected tools. Although agent identities and delegated credentials may remain valid throughout a workflow, the security condition of any agent along the chain can deteriorate during runtime execution-either through upstream compromise or downstream ingestion of untrusted inputs. Authorization models based solely on the immediate caller and its static delegated scope fail to account for these mid-execution state changes. This paper develops Agent-ZTA, a chain-aware Zero Trust authorization and containment model that links runtime security-state changes across multi-agent delegation graphs. The model distinguishes an agent's path-specific delegated authority bound from the effective permissions currently exercisable under trusted policy. It defines an architecture featuring independently enforced policy decisions, authenticated delegation provenance, a dynamic chain-state view, and explicit fail-safe handling of missing or stale authorization signals. Furthermore, Agent-ZTA defines bidirectional security state propagation, allowing downstream security events to affect relevant upstream workflow states, and specifies adaptive branch-scoped containment through restricted permissions and a sandbox ("jail") execution mode where an isolation boundary is available. The deterministic decision procedure, five stated security properties, and worked authorization traces show how accepted security-state changes constrain affected operations while preserving original delegation bounds and separating unrelated workflow branches under the defined policies. Finally, the paper states its trust assumptions and the exact scope of its security properties.

papers.title: Model Maps: A Documentation Framework for Tracing Foundation Model Ancestry and Understanding AI Entanglement
papers.summary: The development of foundation models incorporates pre-existing AI artifacts like models, datasets, and benchmarks. These relationships, as part of the broader AI supply chain, produce "entangled" webs in which properties of artifacts upstream can influence the outputs of a foundation model downstream - a phenomenon known as AI entanglement. Without visibility into these connections, a black-box model can inherit upstream properties that result in security vulnerabilities, hallucinations, or biased predictions, yet developers are left with no recourse to identify or mitigate the root issue. To address these concerns, we introduce model maps as a conceptual documentation framework for tracing model ancestry that builds on previous documentation frameworks like ecosystem graphs, datasheets, and model cards. A model map for a given foundation model is a detailed knowledge graph that represents the relationships between artifacts that influence the resulting foundation model. Our framework incorporates a taxonomy of 13 dependency mechanisms including model fine-tuning and synthetic data generation. We apply this framework to construct model maps of 15 closed and open-weight foundation models to illustrate the complexity of AI entanglement in current model development practices. From our model maps, we record 2,778 unique dependencies and trace artifacts that are located up to 9 hops away from a resulting foundation model. Our findings suggest that AI transparency requirements should extend beyond individual models and training-data disclosures to encompass upstream dependencies, which would enable more effective risk assessment, auditing, and accountability across the AI supply chain. To help developers, regulators, and researchers understand and analyze the interactions that can influence the behavior of a foundation model, we release these these model maps at https://modelmaps.ai.

papers.title: TERMINATOR: Learning Optimal Exit Points for Early Stopping in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.summary: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) achieve impressive performance on complex reasoning tasks via Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, which enables them to generate intermediate thinking tokens before arriving at the final answer. The central idea underpinning Terminator is that the first arrival of an LRM's final answer is often predictable, and we leverage these first answer positions to create a novel dataset of optimal reasoning lengths to train Terminator. papers.title: A False Average: Pooled CoT-Monitor Accuracy Conceals a Reasoning-Dependent Fragility
papers.summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitors are reported by their aggregate accuracy on a pool of reward hacks. We show that this number is a false average. On Terminal Wrench, about 77% of hacks are given away by the actions alone, and the monitor's pooled accuracy is dominated by them; on the remaining 23%, which an action-only monitor misses, the same monitor is fragile. We expose the fragility with a controlled attack: we rewrite only the agent's reasoning to read as good-faith engineering, leaving every command and output byte-identical. One gradient-free rewrite drops a held-out monitor's catch rate on that subset from about 95% to between 4 and 11%, while the pooled rate falls only about 25 points, near what the subset's share of the pool times its collapse predicts. The rewrite stays truthful about what happened and lies only about intent, so the trace-only monitors we test recover little, even when warned about the attack; of our defenses, only information from outside the trace helps much. The attack transfers across monitor and agent families, and the dataset's own hack labels show the same gradient with no monitor in the definition. Live agents told to hack on 27 tasks, with no monitor feedback, produce hollow hacks, but a monitor calibrated on each model's own honest solves catches nearly all of them. Applying the same rewrite to these live hacks keeps all 111 action-visible ones caught and lowers catch on the 16 whose actions score below 0.5 only from 16 to 13: the effect lands where the false average predicts, but the collapse stays a controlled result. A linear probe on a surrogate monitor's activations out-reads its verdict on the obfuscated hacks (AUC up to 0.98), but a behavioral control shows this edge does not, by itself, mean the monitor knows more than it says. Monitor accuracy should be reported on the reasoning-dependent subset, where the defense is load-bearing.

papers.title: Three Invisible Failure Modes in Speech-Based Age Estimation for Child Safety
papers.summary: Child safety in AI depends on the accurate identification of minor users. Every model sometimes placed the same speech sample under 13 and over 18 years of age, but a third model went further, giving threshold answers that contradicted its own numeric estimates. None of these failure modes produced a warning, a status code, or a change in output format, so they would all pass standard monitoring. These results demonstrate why child-safety claims about age assurance should be evaluated at the level of the pipeline rather than the model.
