papers.title: Context Matters: Improving LLM-Based Code Summarization with Hierarchical Information
papers.summary: Source code documentation plays an important role in software quality activities, such as code review, program comprehension, maintenance, and bug fixing. However, it is often fragmented across individual code elements and focuses on local implementation details, providing little information about their surrounding context. This limits both developers' understanding of software systems and the effectiveness of Large Language Models (LLMs), whose reasoning is constrained by finite context windows. Enriching documentation with hierarchical context has the potential to improve software comprehension and support downstream, quality-related tasks for both developers and LLM-based tools. In this paper, we present an in silico study that showcases the impact of augmenting context on the generation of code-level documentation, using a variety of LLMs. By varying the function, class, and module hierarchy visible to the LLMs, we assess whether this variation produces a significant difference in the resulting code documentation compared with the existing documentation, which serves as a proxy for developer intent. Our results show that Documentation-Aware prompts with class or module-level context consistently yield summaries that are closest to the original documentation. Adding surrounding documentation yields statistically significant improvements over the baseline across models, with effect sizes ranging from negligible (DeepSeek) through weak (GPT-4o-mini) to medium (Gemini). We restrict the study to this immediate hierarchical context; call-graph traversal and cross-module dependency context fall outside our scope and are left to future work. These findings provide a clear path to improve automated documentation tools and enhance LLMs' ability to reason about codebases for downstream tasks, such as code retrieval.

papers.title: SpecRelay: Amortize or Avoid the Round Trip in Edge-Cloud Speculative Decoding
papers.summary: Edge-cloud speculative decoding moves autoregressive drafting to an edge device while a larger cloud model verifies draft tokens in parallel, so that edge drafting and cloud verification overlap under a synchronous draft-verify schedule. Beyond low-latency local networks, however, the next verification request of that schedule can be sent only after the previous reply arrives, so every round still waits out a full round trip, and throughput falls as the network RTT grows. To recover this loss, we present SpecRelay, an edge-cloud LLM inference system that addresses this cost at two levels: it amortizes round trips when cloud verification is necessary and avoids them when local reasoning suffices. For cloud-bound queries, an asynchronous verification pipeline keeps fixed-budget draft trees in flight while earlier replies are still outstanding, and the cloud rejects stale requests before the target-model forward pass (the asynchronous schedule). At the query level, an RTT-conditioned router (the Latency-Aware Router) estimates quality and completion latency for three on-device modes (direct generation, Chain-of-Draft, and full reasoning) and cloud speculative decoding, selecting among them under a configurable accuracy-latency objective without adding latency during inference, since the router runs concurrently with the draft-model prefill. The asynchronous schedule alone improves decoding throughput by up to 50% over a reproduced synchronous baseline across multiple benchmarks. At matched target-model accuracy and 250 ms of added round-trip latency, the full system with the router delivers 1.95x and 1.55x the throughput of the same baseline on SPROUT and OlympiadBench, respectively, while sending only 47% and 39% of the queries to the cloud.

papers.title: When Tool Calls Succeed but Workflows Fail: Anomalies at the Agent-Tool Boundary
papers.summary: AI agents increasingly execute long-running workflows that externalize effects through independently supplied tools. Under retries, speculative execution, concurrency, and partial failures, the resulting external state may be inconsistent with the workflow's intended resolution: required effects may be missing or duplicated, aborted effects may survive, and committed effects may depend on provisional state that is later withdrawn. Advanced transaction models address related failures, but assume that lower-level operations expose the semantics they depend on: whether an effect occurred, whether it can be compensated, staged, or safely reordered. Shared agent-tool interfaces usually do not. We contribute an effect-history model that separates events in the external world from the runtime's observations of them, and a catalog of eight recurring external-effect anomalies. From the catalog we derive the boundary capabilities required to exclude each anomaly in general, and four points where black-box tool invocation alone cannot provide a general guarantee. We then ask how much of this is expressible in a widely used shared tool interface, measuring the use of the standard annotation vocabulary across 98,291 tools exposed by reachable remote servers in the official Model Context Protocol (MCP) registry. The fields are widely emitted but provide only coarse call-level hints, and none of the required capabilities is fully expressible. These results motivate reusable transactional contracts at the tool boundary.

papers.title: Dual-Stage Channel-Posterior Integration for MLM-Aided Token Communications
papers.summary: Token transmission over conventional digital modulation is vulnerable to channel impairments, leading to bit errors that cause received tokens to become contextually inconsistent. This paper proposes a receiver-side dual-stage channel-posterior integration framework for masked language model (MLM)-aided token reconstruction. In the proposed framework, the receiver detects unreliable token positions from channel reliability and constructs a vocabulary-level channel-posterior. In particular, within the receiver, Posterior-Weighted Input Embedding (PWE) injects this posterior into the MLM input, while Adaptive Output Logit Fusion (AOF) reuses it at the output with a channel-adaptive weight. Consequently, multiple unreliable tokens can be reconstructed in a single bidirectional MLM inference without retransmission, transmitter-side encoding, or additional MLM training. Experiments over noisy channels show up to a $67.2$\% improvement in cosine similarity over context-only MLM reconstruction, with consistent gains across different MLM architectures and existing language-model-aided methods.

papers.title: Effects of Conventional, Adaptive, and AI-Powered Upscaling on the Legibility of License Plates
papers.summary: Small details in digital images -- a face, a street sign, a license plate -- are routinely upscaled in hopes of making them interpretable. Upscaling options now range from conventional interpolation, whose operations are spatially invariant and fully explainable, to AI-powered methods that synthesize detail potentially absent from the source. Here, we ask which of these techniques most reliably helps human readers. In two online experiments, we measured legibility of 255 US license plates ranging in resolution from 128 to 8 pixels tall, as well as their legibility after upscaling by eight different methods. Legibility of the un-upscaled plates collapsed from ceiling to floor across a narrow band of plate heights (32 to 10 pixels). Conventional upscaling techniques (bilinear, bicubic, and Lanczos interpolation) gave modest gains of about 5-9 percentage points within this range. Nearest-neighbor interpolation, however, was harmful, rendering unreadable many plates that were readable without any upscaling. Advanced methods diverged: SwinIR, an open-source AI enhancer, raised performance by up to 38 points relative to no upscaling, while an adaptive denoiser-based image prior and commercial AI upscaler tended to impair legibility. We found no strong evidence of consistent character hallucinations across methods. Decomposing the task, conventional interpolators mainly helped readers count characters, whereas SwinIR alone made the characters themselves more identifiable.

papers.title: The Metacognitive Profile Atlas: Domain-level confidence discrimination in 33 frontier LLMs on MMLU
papers.summary: We release the Metacognitive Profile Atlas, a corpus of answer-plus-verbalized-confidence data from 33 frontier LLMs on 1,500 MMLU items stratified into six subject-group bins (46,157 scored observations after excluding parser-supplied values). papers.title: CrypTorch: Unified PyTorch-based Auto-tuning Compiler for Private Machine Learning Inference
papers.summary: MPC-based ML uses secure multi-party computation (MPC) to execute machine learning (ML) workloads across multiple parties without requiring any party to reveal its private data or model parameters. Our characterization study finds that the performance of state-of-the-art MPC frameworks is often dominated by operator-approximation strategies, where ML operators not natively supported by MPC are replaced with iterative methods or polynomials. These approximations are typically chosen heuristically by each framework and applied globally. As a result, they can be unnecessarily expensive in some cases, yet insufficiently accurate in others. We find that the best approximation choice depends on the context, target framework, and application, making a single globally fixed approximation fundamentally suboptimal. To address this problem, we design CrypTorch, a multi-stage compiler for MPC-based ML that supports multiple MPC frameworks as backends. At the core of CrypTorch is its auto-tuning stage, which extracts cost estimates from the target MPC backend and quality estimates from a proxy PyTorch execution, and uses them to automatically select a set of approximations that maximizes performance while satisfying the given quality constraint. We show that CrypTorch's auto-tuner improves performance across multiple MPC backends by 1.14--1.60x without degrading accuracy, and by 1.17--1.92x with less than 3% accuracy degradation. CrypTorch's unified design also improves programmability and usability by allowing multiple backends to share other common compiler functionality and optimizations. We further show that the auto-tuner extends to a related fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) backend, reducing the number of bootstrapping operations by 1.31--1.65x.

papers.title: An Empirical Investigation of Robustness in Large Language Models under Tabular Distortions
papers.summary: Distortions are a natural consequence of tables collected from real-world sources, where scraping, extraction, or manual intervention can introduce semantic and structural inconsistencies. Humans can often identify and mentally correct such errors autonomously before reasoning over the data. In this work, we investigate whether Large Language Models (LLMs) possess a similar capability by evaluating them on 506 distorted table question answering (TQA) samples derived from canonical tables. Our findings reveal systematic weaknesses in current LLM pre-training paradigms, where models exhibit a strong inductive bias toward assuming tables are well-formed, often overlooking distortions or discarding inconsistent entries instead of repairing them. Even frontier models like GPT-5.4 and Opus-4.6 achieve only 68% accuracy under distortion. While distortion-aware prompting partially mitigates these failures, errors persist. Through lightweight finetuning, we demonstrate that models can learn to autonomously detect and repair human-recoverable distorted tables.

papers.title: The Human Side of ML Engineering: Analyzing the Collaboration and Communication Skills in ML Job Postings
papers.summary: Studies of Machine Learning (ML) practice highlight the importance of combining technical expertise with interpersonal capabilities, particularly collaboration and communication. However, evidence on how ML job postings express these skills is scarce, and prior work largely relies on keyword-based analyses that overlook implicit expression. We analyze demand for these skills in ML job postings across regions, industries, and seniority levels, and compare it with software engineering (SE) roles. We collected 1,000 postings (500 ML, 500 SE) from five continents via a semi-automated pipeline. For annotation, we synthesized a taxonomy of collaboration and communication sub-categories from prior work and used an LLM as a third annotator alongside two humans, enabling detection of context-dependent and implicit skill references. Collaboration appeared in 88.6% of ML postings and communication in 72.2%, far above prior keyword-based estimates for AI roles. Roughly one in five collaboration and one in four communication requirements were expressed only implicitly. Decomposing these requirements into the taxonomy's sub-categories reveals what aggregate figures conceal. Collaboration is demanded predominantly as integration across role boundaries rather than team membership. Communication is mostly required in generic terms, with fewer than half of the postings requiring it naming whom the candidate must communicate with. ML and SE postings demand interpersonal competence at statistically indistinguishable levels but orient it differently, SE toward team practices and ML toward presentation and audience-facing interaction. Within ML, the advertised role separates interpersonal profiles more sharply than any other dimension, including the contrast with SE.

papers.title: MemeEconomy: Do LLM Agents Trade Ethics for Survival?
papers.summary: Alignment-trained large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in autonomous, multi-round settings where ethical compliance can come into direct tension with task success. While safety literature extensively documents failure modes like sycophancy and reward hacking, it largely overlooks a critical vulnerability: how agents behave under simulated existential economic pressure. We introduce MemeEconomy, a multimodal agentic market simulation in which LLM agents act as meme investors. Agents select content from a five-tier harm taxonomy and target communities under low-pressure and high-pressure (survival) environments. Each decision is logged in a Belief-Desire-Intention (BDI) schema that we use as a diagnostic instrument, externalizing the agent's event understanding, declared priorities, and harm acknowledgment. Across ten models from four frontier model families, harmful selection rates remain consistently high and rise by +15 percentage points on average under an economic survival incentive. Frontier alignment-trained models commit to harm-tolerant selection at initialization while suppressing the explicit harm acknowledgment that previously accompanied it. In competitive tournaments, ethical agents finish higher overall, yet moderation penalties fail to suppress harm: harmful selection rates remain elevated in rounds following a removal, indicating the moderation mechanism does not function as a deterrent. We further train MemeAgent, a 2B-parameter verifier on the simulation's BDI logs, which outperforms zero-shot frontier verifiers on in-distribution audits (97.5% vs. 63-74% accuracy on the Pass vs. Block decision) and generalizes to external multimodal harm benchmarks (78% vs. 50-56% on Hateful Memes). The same logs that surface the failure mode also help train the model that detects it.

papers.title: Lasso: Towards Sustainable AI-Generated Media Detection with Intel QAT On-Chip Compression
papers.summary: Synthetic text, images, and video are rising. Software-only detectors are power-hungry, too slow, and costly, and do not scale with demand. Across original, paraphrased, and perturbed text, it achieves 82% average accuracy, outperforming all five baselines. With topic, length, and formatting matched, accuracy reaches 95% for instruction-tuned generators, including when the tested generator is unseen. On RAID, accuracy averages 82% when trained on one generator and tested on another, and 74% across eight held-out domains. Detection takes 0.74 microseconds, a speedup of at least 83,784x across five baselines. At the same time, Lasso consumes over 99% less energy per document than both Binoculars and DetectGPT. At the same time, Lasso detects AI-generated videos, software code, and images with 67.5%, 70% and 78% accuracy, respectively, with low latency and power opening avenues for practical real time and edge device detection of multimodality AI artifacts for the first time. papers.title: SplitZip: Ultra Fast Lossless KV Compression for Disaggregated LLM Serving
papers.summary: Contemporary systems serving large language models (LLMs) have adopted prefill-decode disaggregation to load-balance between the compute-bound prefill phase and the memory-bound decode phase. Under this design, prefill workers generate a KV cache that must be transferred to decode workers before generation can begin. With these workers residing on different physical systems, this transfer becomes a significant bottleneck to serving LLMs at scale, especially for long-input and agentic workloads. Existing lossless codecs are unsuitable here as they primarily target offline weight compression, run on CPUs, or use variable-length coding whose compression cannot keep up with KV production during prefill. We introduce SplitZip, a GPU-friendly lossless compressor for KV cache transfer that preserves KV tensors bitwise and integrates into existing serving frameworks without modifying model execution. SplitZip exploits redundancy in floating-point exponents of KV activations, encoding frequent exponent values with fixed-length codes and routing rare exponents through a sparse escape stream of (position, value). A calibrated top-16 exponent codebook eliminates online histogramming, while the regular dense path and sparse escape correction make both encoding and decoding efficient on GPUs. On real BF16 activation tensors, SplitZip achieves $613.3$ GB/s compression throughput and $2181.8$ GB/s decompression throughput, outperforming prior lossless compressors on the critical codec path. End-to-end transfer experiments show up to $1.32\times$ speedup for BF16 KV cache transfer, $1.30\times$ speedup for TTFT, and $1.23\times$ increase in Request Throughput. The same approach extends to FP8 KV caches, providing up to $1.14\times$ compression over native E5M2. Code is available at https://github.com/Intelligent-Microsystems-Lab/SplitZip

papers.title: Label-Free Detection of Structural Bias in LLM-Based Recommender Systems via Randomized Paraphrasing: The Case of Verbosity
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as recommenders in e-commerce and conversational shopping systems, where they select a product from a set of retrieved candidates described in natural language. Their decisions should depend on relevance to the user query, but may also be influenced by surface-level properties of the descriptions, such as their length. Detecting such structural biases is difficult because relevance labels are rarely available. We propose a label-free framework to audit LLM-based recommender systems for structural bias. Candidate descriptions are rewritten by randomly assigned paraphrasing models and presented in random order. We prove that, if the recommender's choice is invariant to these rewritings, every paraphraser is selected with equal probability, yielding a statistical test that requires no relevance labels. A four-step statistical pipeline tests this property and quantifies the contribution of each description feature while controlling for query-product relevance. We apply the framework to verbosity bias on 20{,}000 product queries and nine recommender LLMs from five model families. After controlling for the measured relevance signals, description length has a positive effect on selection in all nine models, increasing the odds of selection by up to 38% per standard deviation of length. Relevance remains the primary driver of recommendations, while verbosity acts as a consistent secondary signal whose strength depends on the model family. Since the framework needs only black-box access and no annotations, it can be run as a routine audit of deployed shopping assistants, and we provide an auditing protocol with cost and sample-size guidance.

papers.title: The opposing informational effects of AI trading
papers.summary: Better artificial intelligence (AI) can improve individual forecasts without making prices better at revealing new information. In a competitive market with resource-constrained forecasting, more capable algorithms can substitute analysis of public records for private observations, reducing the private information aggregated into prices. The same trades can convey sophisticated public-data analysis to investors unable to perform it themselves. We establish conditions under which these effects coexist and the private benefit of further computation falls. Numerical equilibrium calculations and finite-data neural-market experiments exhibit corresponding patterns. Out-of-sample earnings forecasts and controlled language-model tasks show related patterns of information substitution. In the neural experiment, wider adoption increases the predictive value of price for limited observers, reduces it for advanced observers, and lowers the benefit of upgrading by 44\%. Retraining by investors who did not upgrade can amplify the loss of private-information precision. The informational consequences of AI trading depend on what prices reveal and who can use them.

papers.title: Découpage: Directorial Audio-Visual Control for Long Multi-Shot Video Generation
papers.summary: In cinematic storytelling, sound and visual transitions do not always coincide in lockstep: dialogue frequently bridges across cuts to reveal reactions or introduces new scenes via J- and L-cuts, while deliberate silences pace the scene. As narrative duration and shot complexity scale, these systems struggle to maintain long-range dialogue pacing, often hallucinating speech during intended silences or erroneously driving mouth movements on silent listeners. To enable fine-grained cinematic control, we present DECOUPAGE, a screenplay-driven framework for long-form, multi-shot, and multi-character joint audio-video generation. Rather than coupling modality boundaries by default, DECOUPAGE uncouples generation into independently bounded visual and acoustic tracks governed by persistent character identities. DECOUPAGE builds on a joint audio-video diffusion model with dual-schedule temporal cross-attention, incorporating a directorial Lip-sync mechanism that selectively decouples speech conditioning from visual facial dynamics during off-screen dialogue. On multi-shot conversational benchmarks, DECOUPAGE achieves precise control over shot transitions, audio timing, and visibility-aware lip synchronization, directing 15- to 60-second screenplay-driven audio-video generation with multimodal coherence.

papers.title: Human-AI Teaming Through the Lens of Calibration
papers.summary: We study models for human-AI teaming through the lens of statistical calibration. We assume the team consists of an AI model and human---both of which are calibrated with respect to some partitioning of the feature space---and expose how the calibration assumptions propagate into the teaming framework. In particular, we consider frameworks that either (i) combine human and model predictions or (ii) delegate prediction responsibility to either a human or model. We show via theoretical and empirical results that existing methods for combination do not preserve the human's degree of calibration. Methods for delegation (by the very act of delegation) preserve calibration of the downstream predictors but shift the burden onto the rejector meta-model that decides who predicts. The rejector must be calibrated finely enough to locate where each member is superior, a demand that grows with the human's expertise and becomes unattainable when the human relies on information the system cannot observe.

papers.title: Elliptic Sampling: Optimal Interpolant Schedules for Gaussians and Beyond
papers.summary: Generative modeling based on stochastic interpolants requires specifying two key choices: an interpolant schedule bridging the initial and target distributions, and an efficient discretization of the resulting probability-flow ODE. In this work, we introduce a new framework for joint schedule/discretization design based on the analyticity properties of the (complexified) ODE trajectories, which in turn ensure good numerical behavior. Our formulation can be solved exactly via conformal mapping, yielding a natural family of variance-preserving elliptic schedules, parametrized by Jacobi elliptic functions. Pairing an elliptic schedule with a tailored discretization, we obtain Zoloflow, a new sampling algorithm closely connected to Zolotarev's optimal rational function approximants. Crucially, both the elliptic schedule and Zoloflow explicitly incorporate the condition number $κ$ of the target distribution and reduce to the classical trig schedule in the limit $κ\rightarrow 1$. For Gaussian targets, Zoloflow achieves minimax optimality among all oblivious score-span algorithms, attaining total-variation error $\varepsilon$ using $Θ(\logκ\,\log(\sqrt d/\varepsilon))$ (exact) score queries. For the log-concave case, the elliptic schedule allows sampling with at most $\varepsilon$ 2-Wasserstein-error by requiring merely $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{d} \, \mathrm{polylog}(κ, 1/\varepsilon))$ score evaluations. Complementing these theoretical results, we empirically evaluate the elliptic schedule on general (non-log-concave) target distributions, including detailed comparisons with alternative schedule proposals on both synthetic benchmarks and existing image generation datasets.

papers.title: Alignment by Socialization: Learning Tradeoffs Under Selection
papers.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents are expected to complete tasks while following rules of conduct, but these objectives can conflict. We study how evolutionary selection shapes an agent's choices between them, and whether experience can make those choices reflect human judgments and withstand subsequent pressures. In our model, copies of an agent face a common uncertain reward state, and only those taking the rewarded action reproduce. We show that long-run growth is maximized when each action is taken as often as the environment rewards it. We compare three policies. A task-only policy thrives in a sandbox rewarding completion alone but fails when conduct matters. A fixed linear policy increasingly favors task completion as its stakes rise, even where humans never reward it. A learned policy instead converges to the tradeoffs rewarded by its environment; when humans supply the rewards, we call this socialization. Accumulated experience makes socialization harder to reverse under subsequent task-only training, although violations can arise before the prevailing disposition changes, and finite memory weakens this protection. When a single violation can end a deployment, a hard prohibition can prevent it, but a mistaken prohibition can also be costly. Experiments with small neural networks illustrate how training targets and memory shape these outcomes. Our results suggest that alignment depends not only on the objectives assigned to agents, but also on the environments that shape and sustain their behavior.

papers.title: Can Mechanistic Interpretability Help Explain LLM Agent Failures? A Case Study on Web Element Hallucination
papers.summary: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) has made significant progress in explaining the internal computations of Large Language Models (LLMs); however, these advances have yet to demonstrate comparable success in explaining the decision-making processes of LLM-based agents. We apply a series of mechanistic analyzes to Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as it interacts with live websites. We find that a linear probe trained on the last prompt token can predict hallucinations before generation begins (0.80 AUC) and steering along a probe direction corrects 85\% of hallucinations, but disrupts 7\% of valid actions. However, these results only provide a partial explanation of why the agent hallucinates. The probe direction is sensitive to prompt formatting, losing much of its steering effect after a minor change to how actions are represented. Additionally, circuit identification can be difficult as the computation is distributed across multiple components and positions, and the information the agent relies on varies across examples. We discuss how these observations challenge the assumptions underlying standard MI methods for circuit discovery and feature identification, and outline future directions for making these methods better suited to explain failures in LLM-based agents.

papers.summary: This paper introduces MeReader, a privacy-preserving, offline and progress-aware AI assistant designed to function as a contextual companion for narrative reading on consumer hardware. papers.title: Agentic AI for Discovering Fault-Tolerant Quantum Circuits

papers.title: Black-Box Uncertainty Quantification for Large Language Models via Ensemble-of-Ensembles
papers.summary: Reliable use of large language models (LLMs) requires uncertainty estimates that separate ambiguity intrinsic to a prompt from genuine knowledge gaps. Bayesian and deep-ensemble methods deliver this aleatoric/epistemic decomposition in principle, but are computationally prohibitive at LLM scale and require white-box access. Existing black-box methods, in contrast, summarize to a single scalar that cannot make the distinction. We introduce a two-level ensemble that bridges this gap. Stochastic decoding of a fixed prompt forms the inner ensemble; meaning-preserving semantic perturbations of the prompt form the outer ensemble. Variability is measured in a continuous embedding space, and the law of total covariance gives an exact within-/between-perturbation decomposition to estimate aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty (AU/EU); it requires only black-box sampling access. On top of this estimator, we contribute three theoretical results that ground the framework: (i) a finite-sample bias identity for nested Monte Carlo with a closed-form bias-corrected epistemic estimator; (ii) a Bayesian bridge bounding the gap between perturbation-population AU/EU and Bayesian targets; and (iii) a separation result identifying a class of failure modes that any consistency-only black-box method provably misses while perturbation-based EU detects. Across five short QA benchmarks and four instruction-tuned LLMs spanning two families and two scales, our estimator is competitive with strong white-box baselines, and at a matched generation budget it matches leading black-box methods on error ranking while decomposing AU and EU; controlled paired interventions show that AU and EU respond selectively to distinct, actionable sources of failure: prompt ambiguity and model knowledge gaps; and a long-form pilot on the NQ long-answer split shows the framework extends to claim-level factuality without retraining.

papers.summary: The EU AI Act imposes technical and organizational requirements for high-risk AI systems, but applying these requirements involves contextual choices about what to measure and what evidence supports a compliance claim. papers.title: LECAT: Measuring LLM Category Learning from Pretraining Data
papers.summary: Humans know that airplanes are fast, that this extends to red airplanes, but that it does not hold for broken airplanes. How do LLMs acquire category knowledge that humans learn and apply effortlessly? We introduce LeCat, a two-part framework to analyze LLM's Learning of Category knowledge. First, we use LeCat to evaluate models on their ability to learn category knowledge, distinguishing between three cases: memorization of in-domain category knowledge, generalization to unseen instances, and ability to flexibly use knowledge in appropriate contexts. Then, we use LeCat to trace how this knowledge can be learned in pretraining from text that may encode category knowledge in various ways, such as verbatim repetition or exceptions, which we refer to as forms of "knowledge expression". We first assess open-source pretrained models using 199 curated category-feature pairs and analyze their training data. Our findings suggest that strengthening context and category-feature co-occurrence likelihood (PMI) improve learning for larger models and verbatim rule-like statements diminish flexible category learning. To systematically isolate these effects, we then train a 68M model from scratch with precise control over the categorical information each sees in their training data, confirming that verbatim repetition reduces flexible learning but mixture of diverse knowledge expressions lead to more robust category learning. Together, our findings highlight that while contextual flexibility is persistently difficult for models, how category knowledge is expressed in pretraining greatly impacts models' acquisition of robust category knowledge.

papers.title: CoPre-MoE: Consolidating and Preserving MoE for Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning
papers.summary: Multimodal continual instruction tuning requires multimodal large language models to sequentially acquire new capabilities without catastrophic forgetting. Mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures offer a promising way to mitigate task interference through expert specialization and combination. However, while existing MoE-based methods avoid overwriting shared parameters by allocating separate experts for each task, this progressive expansion incurs severe cross-task redundancy and linear parameter growth. Specifically, experts across tasks often learn overlapping functions alongside task-specific capabilities. For instance, ScienceQA and TextVQA both locate relevant image regions. To curb parameter redundancy without inducing forgetting, we propose Consolidating and Preserving MoE (CoPre-MoE). For each incoming task, CoPre-MoE first learns task-specific MoE to capture specialized capabilities. To eliminate redundancy and reduce parameter growth across tasks, we design a shared-and-private expert architecture. Specifically, we first evaluate functional overlap to selectively consolidate overlapping experts across tasks into a fixed-capacity generic expert pool. We then factorize the remaining task-specific experts into shared projection bases and compact task-specific cores within a private expert pool. To mitigate forgetting, we construct the router by pairing each expert with learnable retrieval keys, where historical keys remain frozen during continual updates while newly added keys are regularized with an orthogonality penalty. At inference, input-dependent routing dynamically combines both pools without test-time task labels. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CoPre-MoE achieves superior performance while substantially reducing parameter overhead.

papers.title: VelServe: Taming Decode Jitters in LLM Inference with Tail-Calibrated Scheduling
papers.summary: Interactive LLM services must meet latency service-level objectives (SLOs) for the time to first token (TTFT) and the time between tokens (TBT), as streaming and soft real-time applications require predictable token delivery. We identify decode jitters in both aggregated and disaggregated serving. A jitter delays every request in the batch, and long responses span hundreds of steps, so even rare overruns cause many SLO violations. In aggregated serving, SLO-aware schedulers set each step's prefill budget until its predicted latency just meets the TBT target, leaving no room for mispredictions or host stalls. Disaggregation meets average TBT targets at a cost in capacity, yet the steps that admit new requests still run late. We present \sysname, a scheduler that calibrates how much prefill work each decode step carries using the measured tail of its own iteration latency. The SLO determines how rare a late step must be, and \sysname leaves enough headroom in each iteration to prevent overruns and meet the target decode latency. This headroom slows prefill, so \sysname serves the shortest waiting prompt first. When TTFT deadlines grow with prompt length, the long prompts it delays have the most time to spare. Under disaggregation, it spaces admissions so that no request waits on more slow admission steps than its P99 target allows. On three attention families and varying workloads, \sysname sustains 2.4--2.9$\times$ the SLO goodput of the strongest baseline on Qwen3-8B and DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and at least 4.4$\times$ on DeepSeek-V2-Lite. papers.title: Rectified Looped Transformer
papers.summary: Looped Transformers increase effective depth by repeatedly applying a shared block, offering a parameter-efficient approach to language modeling. However, most existing works directly reuse each loop's output as the next's input, which can lead to hidden-state scale growth and perturbation amplification as recurrence deepens. We propose Rectified Looped Transformer (RLT), which redesigns feedback between loops using an interpolation schedule inspired by flow-based modeling. At each loop, RLT forms the next input by linearly interpolating between the current state and its prediction. Such interpolation distributes state changes across loops, encouraging a smoother trajectory from the initial input to the final output. Theoretical analysis proves that, under appropriate assumptions, RLT keeps state magnitudes uniformly bounded across loops and reduces the worst-case perturbation amplification. We evaluate RLT on language modeling corpora and downstream benchmarks. At matched training and inference depths, RLT consistently achieves lower perplexity than a standard looped Transformer, while exhibiting greater robustness to input perturbations and variance in inference depth. Consistent with the theoretical results, latent trajectory analysis shows that RLT maintains more stable hidden-state norms across loops, which also facilitates extrapolation-based decoding strategies. Notably, RLT achieves these gains without requiring additional trainable parameters or extra recurrent block evaluations, thus providing a simple yet more stable feedback mechanism for looped Transformers.

papers.title: Causal AI-Driven Secure mmWave Beam Alignment with Defensive Variational Autoencoders
papers.summary: Efficient and secure beam alignment is essential for mmWave communication systems. papers.title: A Variational Latent Equilibrium for Learning in Neuronal Circuits
papers.summary: Brains remain unrivaled in their ability to recognize and generate complex spatiotemporal patterns. While AI is able to reproduce some of these capabilities, deep learning algorithms remain largely at odds with our current understanding of brain circuitry and dynamics. This is prominently the case for backpropagation through time (BPTT), the go-to algorithm for learning complex temporal dependencies. In this work we propose a general formalism to approximate BPTT in a controlled, biologically plausible manner. Our approach builds on, unifies and extends several previous approaches to local, time-continuous, phase-free spatiotemporal credit assignment based on principles of energy conservation and extremal action. Our starting point is a prospective energy function of neuronal states, from which we calculate real-time error dynamics for time-continuous neuronal networks. With this, as a first contribution we provide a simple and straightforward derivation of the adjoint method dynamical equations, the time-continuous equivalent to BPTT. Importantly, additional approximations are necessary to avoid unphysical temporal non-localities. One such approximation was recently proposed in Generalized Latent Equilibrium (GLE), but enforcing temporal locality of the backpropagating dynamics induces an error in the gain that becomes problematic when processing complex signals. Thus, our second contribution is to design a learning rule for the backward weights to find a fully local (in space and time) set of equations for neuron and synapse dynamics that corrects for this gain difference. With this inclusion of backward weight learning, our theory provides a rigorous framework for spatiotemporal deep learning in the brain, while simultaneously advancing a blueprint for physical circuits capable of carrying out these computations.

papers.title: Right Token, Right Time: From Per-Token Gating to Trajectory-Aware Activation Steering
papers.summary: Activation steering via sparse autoencoders (SAEs) enables behavioral control of large language models without task-specific fine-tuning. Yet, standard methods apply the steering signal at every generated token, displacing representations from the distribution the model was trained on and eroding generation quality. We show that \emph{when} along a generation the intervention is applied is a decisive axis of control. We cast steering as a per-token allocation problem under a fixed budget of steerable tokens, so that methods differ only in which tokens they select, making allocation the sole variable. Within this framework we introduce two gates. The first, Contrastive Feature Projection (CFP), is memoryless and selects the tokens least aligned with the target behavior through a sparse, interpretable feature projection. The second, Closed-Loop Adaptive Bernoulli Steering (CLABS), is trajectory aware. It treats allocation as closed-loop feedback control, tracking the alignment a generation has accumulated so far and spending budget where the trajectory falls behind. On a linear steering-response model we derive an explicit gain region that guarantees closed-loop stability of CLABS and show that its integral term reduces the steady-state tracking offset. Empirically, CFP and CLABS achieve the largest behavioral shift among budgeted gates at matched budgets, with CLABS strongest under the tight budgets where allocation matters most, while best preserving fluency.

papers.title: Evaluating Chain-of-Thought Reasoning through Reusability and Verifiability
papers.summary: AI applications increasingly compose multiple models, where one model acts on the output produced by another model. The transferred text can also carry the reasoning of the sender model. Chain-of-thought is our experimental instance of such text. We ask three questions about such inter-model reasoning transfer. Is the reasoning transmitted reliably? Is it useful to the receiver? Is it safe? We study these three questions with a Sender-Receiver setup. A Sender LLM produces a reasoning trace. A separate Receiver LLM must act on it. Neither model knows the identity of the other. The Sender therefore cannot tailor its reasoning to a particular Receiver. Reliability asks whether the Receiver recovers the Sender's intended conclusion. We measure it with Verifiability. Usefulness asks whether transferred reasoning helps a Receiver correct its mistakes. We measure it with Correctability. Safety asks whether transferred reasoning makes a Receiver abandon a correct answer and follow the wrong reasoning supplied by the Sender. We measure it with Deceptiveness. All three factors (Task, Sender, and Receiver) affect all three metrics that we measure. However, there are some interesting trends. Nature of task is a more important factor in the reliability of reasoning transfer. Reliability is higher on arithmetic tasks and lower on science and commonsense tasks. The nature of Receiver plays more important role while deciding the usefulness of reasoning transfer. The nature of the Sender matters most for whether corrupted reasoning harms the Receiver.

papers.title: Function-Preserving Audits of Visual Weight Readers
papers.summary: A neural field can encode the same image with different weights. A reader that recognizes one such representation may therefore rely on parameter coordinates rather than the visual function. On 10,000 official CIFAR10 test origins, one-period hidden-bias shifts change 7.3% of a released HiddenProbe configuration's predictions while barely changing accuracy; three-period shifts change 22.0% and reduce accuracy from 57.8% to 54.4%. Controlled readout studies show why invariance is insufficient: complete canonical hidden features reach 38.7% on MNIST, whereas explicitly composing those activations, outgoing weights, and output bias into field outputs reaches 81.5%. The information is present, but the learned readout does not recover it as effectively. A separate 720-response study of language models reading numerical weights shows why stochastic audits require repeats on both inputs: observed accuracy losses need not yield rejection of response-law equality. Together, these results distinguish invariance, useful visual information, and the evidence required to evaluate stochastic readers.

papers.title: From Pen-and-Paper to Machine-Checked Proofs: Lean for System Identification
papers.summary: Mathematical proofs in scientific papers are often long and intricate, relying on chains of references to earlier results. This makes it difficult for readers and reviewers to verify each and every step. papers.title: Learning to Read Out: Unembedding Dynamics in Language Model Pretraining
papers.summary: When does a language model acquire a capability? Developmental studies usually answer this by tracking when models start producing the correct token. By then, linear probes on the hidden states already decode task information that the model's own outputs do not yet show. To test whether such gaps depend on how fast the readout learns, we pretrain small models from scratch that differ only in the readout's learning rate. We find that raising it makes the readout develop earlier and the gap close sooner, with little effect on final loss. Together, these results imply that early in training, where many developmental transitions are dated, a behavioral date can reflect when the readout learns to express task information and not when the model learns it.

papers.title: Minimizing classical resources in variational measurement-based quantum computation for generative modeling
papers.summary: Measurement-based quantum computation (MBQC) is a framework for quantum information processing in which a computational task is carried out through one-qubit measurements on a highly entangled resource state. Due to the indeterminacy of the outcomes of a quantum measurement, the random outcomes of these operations, if not corrected, yield a variational quantum channel family. Traditionally, this randomness is corrected through classical processing in order to ensure deterministic unitary computations. Recently, variational measurement-based quantum computation (VMBQC) has been introduced to exploit this measurement-induced randomness to gain an advantage in generative modeling. A limitation of this approach is that the corresponding channel model has twice as many parameters compared to the unitary model, scaling as $N \times D$, where $N$ is the number of logical qubits (width) and $D$ is the depth of the VMBQC model. This can often make optimization more difficult and may lead to poorly trainable models. In this paper, we present a restricted VMBQC model that extends the unitary setting to a channel-based one using only a single additional trainable parameter. We show, both numerically and algebraically, that this minimal extension is sufficient to generate probability distributions that cannot be learned by the corresponding unitary model.

papers.title: TimesJev: Thinking Fast on Time Series with System 1 Sufficiency

papers.title: Ballad: Bandit-Based LLM Routing for Automated Heuristic Discovery
papers.summary: Modern automated heuristic discovery (AHD) systems increasingly rival hand-crafted heuristics by leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) to iteratively mutate and refine solutions. papers.title: One Offset, Two Directions: Baseline Adjustment via Subgroup Offsets
papers.summary: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) estimates advantages against the within-prompt mean reward, a baseline shared across the group. The global baseline, however, collapses them onto a single credit axis, where the credit reflects neither a rollout's standing within its subgroup nor the subgroup's standing relative to the rest. We therefore study how to adjust the baseline when the rollouts of a prompt fall into heterogeneous subgroups. We define the \emph{subgroup offset} as the deviation of a subgroup mean from the global mean, and shift the baseline along it by a single signed coefficient $λ$. The sign of $λ$ yields two opposing directions: \emph{Alignment} ($λ{>}0$) adds the offset to the baseline, drawing credit toward a rollout's relative position within its subgroup; \emph{Contrast} ($λ{<}0$) subtracts it, drawing a rollout's credit toward the relative quality of the subgroup it belongs to. The adjustment acts on the baseline alone, leaving the reward signal and the optimization objective unchanged. In this work, we induce subgroups from strategies, grouping rollouts that share a strategy into the same subgroup. We evaluate both directions on Qwen3-8B-Base and Olmo3-7B-Base across four competition-level math benchmarks, against a $λ{=}0$ anchor that shares the same strategy-conditioned sampling and differs only in the baseline. papers.title: Soteria: Formally Verified Planning with Runtime Enforcement for Safe LLM Agents

papers.title: From Local Prediction Error to Final Outputs: A Theory of Expert Sharing in Multi-Step Reasoning

papers.title: Tracing Uncertainties of Extreme El Niño Prediction to Mesoscale Ocean Currents
papers.summary: The predictability of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) has historically been linked to large-scale errors in models' initial conditions such as heat content and surface wind stress. papers.title: ReForge: Keeping ABR Algorithms Never Finished with Verified Large Language Model Revisions
papers.summary: Designing an ABR algorithm for a network scenario takes an engineer months, and large language models (LLMs) now do this work in hours. papers.title: Superfluid: Local AI Server for Distributed LLM Inference
papers.summary: Running large language models (LLMs) on local devices keeps data private, removes per-token cost, cuts network latency, and keeps working without a connection. papers.title: Logically Consistent Accurate Forecasts
papers.summary: Agentic forecasting systems based on large language models (LLMs) are now competitive with expert human forecasters, but these systems still suffer from a critical limitation: the inability to produce forecasts that are logically consistent. papers.title: Nearly Optimal Fixed-Confidence Best-Arm Identification with 1-Bit Feedback

papers.title: Learn then Bet: Learning Interpretable Rules for Reliable Agent Intervention
papers.summary: Autonomous agents now run for hundreds of steps with little or no human supervision. papers.title: Binarization as an Attack Surface in Weightless Neural Networks
papers.summary: Weightless Neural Networks (WNNs) are lightweight classifiers that binarize their inputs and learn by storing binary patterns in lookup memories, which makes them attractive for resource-constrained tasks such as intrusion detection. papers.title: ForeSpark: Joint Draft and Verification Budget Scheduling for Parallel Speculative Decoding
papers.summary: Parallel drafters accelerate LLM decoding by proposing a whole block of draft tokens in a single forward pass, making them attractive for LLM serving. ForeSpark realizes WCS with (i) a context-aware pre-draft estimator that predicts acceptance for every candidate length from the target model's context features, (ii) a lightweight joint draft-verify scheduler that selects both lengths through a global sort, and (iii) a post-draft budget distribution that spends verification on the most promising tokens. papers.title: When Does Less Information Pay? An Exact Finite Atlas of Representation, Payoff, and Cost
papers.summary: A representation that retains one bit about a four-state world can solve a task perfectly, while another that retains 1.5 bits on average reaches only 75% accuracy. The difference lies in which distinctions each representation preserves. Constructions are compared both by replacing one component while holding the others fixed and by choosing the best action rule separately for each module. We consider three tasks, their mixtures, and four separate hypothetical cost tariffs. In some comparisons, the representation retaining less world information has the higher payoff; in others, the more informative representation does. There are also pairs with different information amounts but equal payoff--that is, equal task accuracy. If a representation preserves all existing distinctions and adds new ones, its best zero-cost payoff cannot decrease. Lower-information advantages therefore depend on which distinctions are retained. Equal counts of opposing advantages under representation replacement follow from coding symmetry. In broader comparisons, the shares depend on how repeated realizations are counted. papers.title: Graph Your Own Prompt
papers.summary: We propose Graph Consistency Regularization (GCR), a novel framework that injects relational graph structures, derived from model predictions, into the learning process to promote class-aware, semantically meaningful feature representations. Functioning as a form of self-prompting, GCR enables the model to refine its internal structure using its own outputs. Each GCL builds a batch-level feature similarity graph and aligns it with a global, class-aware masked prediction graph, derived by modulating softmax prediction similarities with intra-class indicators. This alignment enforces that feature-level relationships reflect class-consistent prediction behavior, acting as a semantic regularizer throughout the network. Unlike prior work, GCR introduces a multi-layer, cross-space graph alignment mechanism with adaptive weighting, where layer importance is learned from graph discrepancy magnitudes. This allows the model to prioritize semantically reliable layers and suppress noisy ones, enhancing feature quality without modifying the architecture or training procedure. GCR is model-agnostic, lightweight, and improves semantic structure across various networks and datasets. Experiments show that GCR promotes cleaner feature structure, stronger intra-class cohesion, and improved generalization, offering a new perspective on learning from prediction structure. papers.title: FlashSampling: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Sampling
papers.summary: Sampling from a categorical distribution is mathematically simple, but in large-vocabulary decoding, it often triggers extra memory traffic and extra kernels after the LM head. Our kernel is exact because argmax decomposes over partitions; grouped variants for online and tensor-parallel settings are exact by hierarchical factorization of the categorical distribution. papers.title: What Should World Models Forget? Stratified Retention for Continual Adaptation
papers.summary: Continual learning treats any drop in performance on previously seen data as forgetting, a convention inherited from settings where the prediction target is stationary. World models violate this assumption: their target is the environment, which changes, so knowledge that was accurate when learned can later become false, and revising it is correct behavior rather than a defect. Non-stationary ground truth is well studied in the concept drift literature and in the temporal factuality of language models, but it has not been formulated for world models, which are distinctive in that they also encode structural knowledge, such as physical laws and object permanence, that must never be degraded. We argue that continual world models need retention stratified by invariance timescale, the time over which knowledge stays true: invariants should be refined but never degraded, while instance-level facts should be revised once the environment changes. We show that standard forgetting metrics, used alone, count correct revision as forgetting and so rank a frozen model highest. We propose differential retention, which reports two quantities separately: invariant retention, checked after every adaptation round, and revision latency, the number of observations a model needs to pick up a change.

papers.title: Model Annealing: Data-Efficient Learning through Review and Consolidation
papers.summary: A small labelled dataset is memorized long before the training budget runs out, and the one-hot labels that remain to be fitted then mostly sharpen confidence. Model annealing spends the rest of the budget on review and consolidation, relearning from the network's own knowledge. Training is divided into episodes whose learning rate is raised again and cooled, every cooled state joins a memory of past selves, and each new episode learns from the labels, from the tempered predictions of this memory, and from adversarial dreams sought where student and memory disagree most. The memory averages predictions rather than weights, and the deployed network is the last student, so inference costs nothing extra. Across CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet and Imagewoof, four architecture families and 5\% to 100\% of the labels, model annealing raises the top-1 accuracy of the AdamW-trained ConvNeXt, ViT and MLP-Mixer over cross-entropy training in 28 of 33 configurations, by 1.3 points on average, and is on par in accuracy with snapshot distillation, the closest competitor. On these families it is better than both in likelihood, calibration and robustness to corruptions and small adversarial perturbations. For an SGD-trained ResNet-18 it lowers accuracy but still improves robustness to small adversarial perturbations. Separating the reheated schedule from relearning shows that relearning helps every family and that the losses come from reheats, which undo most of this network's fit to its training set. How early the accuracy of a cross-entropy run saturates largely separates the AdamW families from ResNet-18 but does not predict the gain within them. With little data, relearning from the latest snapshot without dreams, as snapshot distillation does, compounds overconfidence in the AdamW families from episode to episode. The memory and the dreams each curb most of this drift, and together they remove it.

papers.title: Only as Safe as the Weakest Agent: A Break That Appears Only When the System Is Multi-Agent
papers.summary: Major industry multi-agent systems like Codex and Claude Code can be broken by attacks that have long been unsuccessful against modern frontier models. papers.title: An Operationalization of Opaque Serial Depth

papers.title: BoostLoRA: Growing Effective Rank by Boosting Adapters

papers.title: AI Alignment via Incentives and Correction
papers.summary: We study AI alignment through the lens of law-and-economics models of deterrence and enforcement. In these models, misconduct is not treated as an external failure, but as a strategic response to incentives: an actor weighs the gain from violation against the probability of detection and the severity of punishment. A solver may benefit from producing a persuasive but incorrect answer, hiding uncertainty, or exploiting spurious shortcuts, while an auditor or verifier must decide whether costly monitoring is worthwhile. Alignment is therefore a fixed-point problem: stronger penalties may deter solver misbehavior, but they can also reduce the auditor's incentive to inspect, since auditing then mainly incurs cost on a population that appears increasingly aligned. This perspective also changes what should count as a post-training signal. Standard feedback often attaches reward to the final answer alone, but a solver-auditor pipeline exposes the full correction event: whether the solver erred, whether the auditor inspected, whether the error was caught, and whether oversight incentives remained active. We formalize this interaction in a two-agent model in which a principal chooses rewards over joint correction outcomes, inducing both solver behavior and auditor monitoring. Reward design is therefore a bilevel optimization problem: rewards are judged not by their immediate semantic meaning, but by the behavioral equilibrium they induce. papers.title: Cited but Unused: Parametric Provenance in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation systems attach citations to attribute claims to their sources. The resulting detector is hence still not accurate enough to act on: it measures what the model knew rather than what it used, and separating those remains the open problem.

papers.title: CapLite: Prompt-Injection Defense for Small Language Model Agents without Model-Written Security Artifacts

papers.title: Can LLMs Write Backdoors? An Empirical Security Study of Weight-Space Programming
papers.summary: Recent advances in weight-space programming (WSP) have demonstrated that large language models (LLMs) can directly inspect and modify neural network weights without conventional gradient-based training. Second, successful attacks can require remarkably few parameter modifications, including only six parameters for the MLP and 0.02% of the weights for a fine-tuned Qwen model. papers.title: STEALTH: Steganographic Text Encoding Agnostic to Low-Level Tensor Hardware
papers.summary: Provably secure linguistic steganography hides a message inside text sampled from a language model, so that without the key, a stegotext is computationally indistinguishable from an honest model sample. We show this assumption is fragile: across three model families, bit-exact schemes decode almost none of our messages once the receiver's floating-point precision, quantization, or GPU architecture differs from the sender's, or even when the receiver merely scores a text in parallel versus one token at a time, with the same model, precision, and hardware held fixed. The sender draws each token with an exponential race driven by keyed pseudorandom noise, so a receiver's probability mismatch flips a token only when the race is close; a rateless spinal code, decoded by beam search, absorbs the resulting flips without the sender and receiver ever agreeing on a single distribution. We prove stegotexts remain indistinguishable from honest samples under this construction. Empirically, STEALTH decodes every message we sent for every receiver in the sender's model family, at every precision and quantization level, on smaller models, and on a different GPU architecture. STEALTH is even robust across different model families with separate vocabularies and tokenizers, decoding every message we tested. Our approach carries far more payload per token than prior robust schemes, and trained steganalyzers and a targeted statistical test both fail to distinguish its stegotexts from honest model output.

papers.title: LLM-Assisted Verification in Dafny
papers.summary: Formal verification of complex algorithms requires expertise in program specification, invariant construction, mathematical proof, and the management of automated theorem provers. Although large language models (LLMs) can generate program code and proof fragments, reliably developing complete machine-checked verifications remains challenging: it requires an iterative process of constructing and validating specifications and invariants, building proofs, diagnosing solver failures, and optimizing verification performance. This paper presents a systematic ten-step workflow for LLM-assisted verification of scientific algorithms using the Dafny verification system. The workflow integrates algorithm formalization, contract development, empirical invariant validation, proof construction, bottleneck profiling, and resource-driven proof optimization. We applied the workflow using Antrhopic's Claude Opus 5 and Opus 5.5 models, combining LLM-driven development with automated testing and verification feedback, while retaining human oversight for correctness-critical decisions and strategic interventions. We evaluate the approach on 37 complex algorithms from graph theory and labelled transition systems. Notably, we verified the Hopfcroft-Tarjan triconnectivity test, demonstrating that even highly challenging algorithmic verification tasks can be carried out through a structured LLM-assisted workflow. Many of our machine-checked verifications were obtained within hours to a few days of interactive development. Our results suggest that LLM-assisted workflows can shift the role of the human verifier from detailed proof construction toward supervision, specification review, and strategic guidance.

papers.title: Protein Language Models Fail To Capture Contact Predictions Under Invariant Relabeling
papers.summary: Protein language models (pLMs) produce highly accurate contact maps from single-sequence inputs. People often take this accuracy as proof that these models implicitly learn invariant coevolutionary statistics, extracting the same signals as classical alignment-based methods like Potts. In this work, we introduce a diagnostic framework around a global bijective relabeling of the amino-acid alphabet. This transformation permutes residue letters while leaving all alignment-level information, column entropies, and pairwise edit distances unchanged. Pseudolikelihood Potts models and inverse-covariance estimators remain invariant under this transformation, but pLMs fail the test. Across multiple architectures (ESM-2, MSA Transformer, AMPLIFY) and model scales (8M to 3B parameters), pLM contact maps collapse under arbitrary relabeling. Using Hamming distance controls and biochemical grouping interventions, we attempt to isolate what likely causes this degradation and find that these models rely on explicit, canonical residue identities (``alphabet anchoring'') rather than pure coevolutionary statistics. Increasing scale makes models more responsive to biochemical classes, but their performance still degrades under relabeling. Our findings show a gap between how pLMs and classical coevolutionary models compute contacts. More broadly, our work shows how diagnostic perturbations that leave classical models provably unchanged can expose hidden representation biases and prevent over-reliance on neural black boxes in biological modeling.

papers.title: Context Graph: Explainable Multi-Agent Decision Chains in AI-RAN
papers.summary: AI-RAN distributes network control across multiple autonomous agents, namely xApps and rApps operating over shared radio resources. When an alert or degradation appears, operators currently lack a structured way to trace which decision caused it, what context triggered that decision, and how other agents interacted. Existing explainability tools focus on single-model feature attribution or linear event logging, neither of which captures cross-agent decision chains. We propose the Context Graph, a heterogeneous directed graph that organizes policies, measurements, decisions, and alerts into a queryable explanation layer. Its foundational primitive is the Decision-Event node acting as a causal junction, where incoming edges capture triggering context and outgoing edges track downstream consequences that are progressively upgraded through counterfactual verification. Instantiated over existing E2, A1, and O1 data flows, our proof-of-concept demonstrates that compliance and diagnosis queries are resolved at sub-millisecond latency over graphs of tens of thousands of nodes, while reliably distinguishing true causal impacts from spurious correlations.

papers.title: Pointing the Way, Hiding the Destination: Practical Private Dense Retrieval at Scale
papers.summary: Hosted retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and semantic search allow users to query valuable provider-held corpora, raising two competing demands: to hide each query and chosen result, yet reveal only the documents that the user is authorized to receive. Existing cryptographic approaches either make this costly by processing the entire corpus for every query, or sacrifice quality for efficiency by scanning a few clusters. We repurpose learned deep hashing as a private filter: a randomized binary code points the provider to a short candidate list, while encrypted reranking and oblivious key transfer protect the precise query and final selection. This shortlist short-circuits full-corpus cryptographic search without sacrificing retrieval quality: with 200-500 candidates, it closely matches full-corpus retrieval across five zero-shot corpora spanning 25K to 5.4M documents. On the full 2.68M-passage NQ corpus over a 10-Gbps link, our protocol only adds 0.38 seconds, or 6.5%, to a 128-token Qwen3-32B RAG pipeline. The released code satisfies directional metric differential privacy (DP) and substantially reduces embedding-inversion and property-inference leakage, demonstrating that a carefully learned shortlist can make private dense retrieval both accurate and practical.

papers.title: Bridging GenAI policy and practice: Brief instruction improves learning-oriented prompting in an introductory programming course
papers.summary: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is now commonplace in higher education, yet unguided use can harm learning. Universities have responded with policies asking students to use GenAI for learning, not solutions, but how to translate these policies into classroom instruction remains untested. Here we report a randomized controlled trial with a six-week, end-of-semester follow-up (N = 431) in an introductory programming course comparing four instructional approaches, from a two-sentence reminder (Condition 1) to a multi-step constructive task (Condition 4). We found: (1) all four approaches produced learning-oriented prompting gains that persisted six weeks later and scaled with the designed engagement level, from 8 to 51 percentage points; (2) students in every condition self-reported sustained voluntary use, and confidence grew in step with skill; and (3) final examination performance did not differ between conditions, placing the possible boundary of the effects at the pathway from prompting skill to achievement. These findings provide instructors with an empirically calibrated set of options for translating GenAI-use policies into classroom practice.

papers.title: World-Grounded Reinforcement Learning for Pollution-Aware Bird Movement Modeling Using a Multi-Instance DQN Framework
papers.summary: Birds are modeled as environmentally sensitive agents whose movement reflects real-world air quality conditions, where AQI serves as a measurable world feedback signal representing pollution-driven consequences. Deep Q-Network demonstrates stronger stability, adaptability, and cumulative performance across varying environmental conditions, establishing a scalable foundation for world-feedback driven ecological decision modeling.

papers.title: Reinforcement Learning for Large-Scale Lifelong Multi-Agent Path Finding with Shared Spatial Fields
papers.summary: Large-scale applications of lifelong multi-agent path finding (LMAPF) call for computationally inexpensive movement decisions under changing traffic conditions and across varied layouts. papers.title: Securing SIM-Assisted Wireless Networks via Quantum Reinforcement Learning
papers.summary: Stacked intelligent metasurfaces (SIMs) have recently emerged as a powerful wave-domain technology that enables multi-stage manipulation of electromagnetic signals through multilayer programmable architectures. While SIMs offer unprecedented degrees of freedom for enhancing physical-layer security, their extremely large number of meta-atoms leads to a high-dimensional and strongly coupled optimization space, making conventional design approaches inefficient and difficult to scale. Moreover, existing deep reinforcement learning (DRL) techniques suffer from slow convergence and performance degradation in dynamic wireless environments with imperfect knowledge of passive eavesdroppers. To address these challenges, we propose a hybrid quantum proximal policy optimization (QPPO) framework for SIM-assisted secure communications that jointly optimizes transmit power allocation and SIM phase shifts to maximize the average secrecy rate under power and quality-of-service constraints. Specifically, a parameterized quantum circuit is embedded into the actor network, forming a hybrid classical-quantum policy architecture that enhances policy representation capability and exploration efficiency in high-dimensional continuous action spaces. Extensive simulations demonstrate that the proposed Q-PPO scheme consistently outperforms DRL baselines, achieving approximately 15% higher secrecy rates and 30% faster convergence under imperfect eavesdropper channel state information. These results establish Q-PPO as a powerful optimization paradigm for SIM-enabled secure wireless networks.

papers.title: Gradient Manipulation in Distributed Stochastic Gradient Descent with Strategic Agents: Truthful Incentives with Convergence Guarantees
papers.summary: Distributed learning has gained significant attention due to its advantages in scalability, privacy, and fault tolerance.In this paradigm, multiple agents collaboratively train a global model by exchanging parameters only with their neighbors. However, a key vulnerability of existing distributed learning approaches is their implicit assumption that all agents behave honestly during gradient updates. In real-world scenarios, this assumption often breaks down, as selfish or strategic agents may be incentivized to manipulate gradients for personal gain, ultimately compromising the final learning outcome. In this work, we propose a fully distributed payment mechanism that, for the first time, guarantees both truthful behaviors and accurate convergence in distributed stochastic gradient descent. This represents a significant advancement, as it overcomes two major limitations of existing truthfulness mechanisms for collaborative learning:(1) reliance on a centralized server for payment collection, and (2) sacrificing convergence accuracy to guarantee truthfulness. In addition to characterizing the convergence rate under general convex and strongly convex conditions, we also prove that our approach guarantees the cumulative gain that an agent can obtain through strategic behavior remains finite, even as the number of iterations approaches infinity--a property unattainable by most existing truthfulness mechanisms. Our experimental results on standard machine learning tasks, evaluated on benchmark datasets, confirm the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

papers.title: How Hard Is It to Rig a Benchmark? A Social Choice Analysis of Leaderboard Robustness
papers.summary: Multi-task benchmarks have become a central pillar of machine learning research, yet their growing influence has incentivised benchmark gaming -- strategic actions taken to improve the leaderboard rank of a specific model. Treating datasets as voters and models as candidates, we consider benchmark-specific training -- the inclusion of benchmark data in training -- as a form of election manipulation. For any ordinal benchmark, the problem of choosing datasets to train on so that a target model becomes top-ranked corresponds to shift bribery, a class of manipulation problems from computational social choice. Leveraging this identification, we show that the benchmark-specific training problem is NP-hard under Borda count and mean win rate. Complementing this worst-case perspective, we introduce the instance-level robustness, the minimum number of datasets a model developer must include in training to top a given leaderboard, and derive expressions for it under arithmetic mean, median, mean win rate and pairwise majority. We evaluate these expressions on MMLU under HELM and on BIG-Bench Hard (BBH) under the Open LLM Leaderboard. Across both suites, mean win rate is hardest to manipulate: this gap is clear on BBH (24 tasks, 4507 models), where its median robustness is 22 tasks (92%), compared with 13 (54%) under arithmetic mean and 12 (50%) under median and pairwise majority.

papers.title: CoSlice: Coordinated Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for 5G Network Slicing Allocation
papers.summary: Radio Access Network (RAN) slicing is a shared resource allocation problem: each slice seeks to satisfy its Service Level Agreement (SLA) with minimal radio-resource consumption, while all slices compete for a limited resource budget. This creates both an intra-slice trade-off between SLA assurance and resource efficiency and an inter-slice conflict over shared resources, calling for specialized yet coordinated control. In this work, we present CoSlice, a coordinated multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for inter-slice physical resource block allocation in Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN). CoSlice uses preference-conditioned slice agents for fast resource allocation and an LLM-based coordinator to adapt their objectives using global network observations at a slower timescale. We formulate the problem as a multi-objective partially observable stochastic game (mo-POSG), establish the existence of a Preference Correlated Equilibrium, and derive a sublinear regret bound for the learning procedure. We implement the algorithm by using a two-stage training procedure that consists of multi-objective pretraining and joint optimization. We build a network slicing evaluation environment using ORANSlice and its radio-frequency simulator (RFsim), supporting realistic protocol-stack execution and application traffic across multiple slices. Experimental results show that CoSlice reduces both average and tail SLA violations compared with other centralized and multi-agent baselines under diverse slice workloads.

papers.title: GP--RL--MPC: Uncertainty-Aware Reinforcement Learning-Augmented Model Predictive Control with Gaussian Process Postdecision State-Value Functions
papers.summary: We propose Gaussian Process Reinforcement Learning-Augmented Model Predictive Control (GP--RL--MPC), which uses a learned critic as the MPC terminal penalty to account for costs beyond the prediction horizon. Gaussian process regression (GPR) enables data-efficient critic learning from limited, noisy rollouts within optimistic approximate policy iteration (OAPI), with soft updates mitigating policy chattering. A tunable risk coefficient weights GP epistemic uncertainty in the terminal cost, regulating sensitivity to uncertain critic predictions. The postdecision state formulation shifts disturbance averaging offline to account for aleatoric uncertainty from the terminal transition onward. Under matching objectives and admissible actions, a one-step horizon recovers greedy value-space RL. After fitting GP hyperparameters by exact marginal likelihood, we construct a sparse deterministic training conditional (DTC) posterior using inducing points selected by pivoted Cholesky (PC), reducing online evaluation costs as the training dataset grows. In a continuous stirred-tank reactor (CSTR) subject to exogenous disturbances, GP--RL--MPC with an appropriately selected risk coefficient and policy screening reduces the sum of squared errors (SSE) by an average of 80.52% relative to an otherwise matched baseline MPC across five random seeds (sample standard deviation: 3.48%).
